speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DONATION OF WHOLE MILK POWDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that the government has authorized the agricultural products board to make available for international welfare purposes, through approved international relief agencies, a quantity of whole milk powder purchased by the board as part of the program for the utilization of surplus dairy products.
The whole milk powder will be made available to these organizations by the board in consultation with the Department of External Affairs, whose officers are conversant with the various international relief programs. An initial donation of approximately two million pounds is being made available
to the United Nations international children's emergency fund for immediate shipment to 12 different countries.
Because of its butter fat content whole milk powder is one of the commodities most urgently requested by international welfare agencies to assist them in carrying out their welfare programs, particularly in the underdeveloped countries.

subsubtopic: REPORTED REFERRAL OF MEN TO FIRMS IN LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext: I wonder whether the Minister of Labour has a reply to a question I have been raising in the last couple of days concerning a complaint from the British Columbia federation of labour to the national employment service in relation to the hardware firms of Mac and Mac and Marshall Wells?

subsubtopic: REPORTED REFERRAL OF MEN TO FIRMS IN LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
I forwarded to Mr. O'Neal of the British Columbia federation of labour a letter which embodies the report I received from the unemployment insurance commission. The best manner in which I can explain this situation is, with your permission, to read the letter which I addressed to Mr. O'Neal. It reads: With reference to your telegram of July 7, I may say that I have asked the regional director of the unemployment insurance commission to ensure that

commission policy concerning the referral of workers to employment that is affected by an industrial dispute is being fully observed in the case to which you refer.
In these matters the commission's policy is to maintain a position of strict impartiality as between employers and workers. In doing this, the commission accepts employers' orders and refers applicants. But in offering referral, applicants are carefully advised in every instance that the employment is involved in a dispute and further that because of this, refusal to accept the referral will have no effect whatever on either the applicant's right to benefit or his right to other referrals. Applicants are then referred only in those cases where they express a desire to apply for the employment in question. Moreover, where workers on strike or locked out seek alternative employment, whether permanent or temporary, employment offices will in those cases not refuse to serve the applications of such workers.
This policy stems from the commission's obligation to find employment for applicants who register and to find workers for employers who list vacancies-as long as in doing so the commission violates no legal requirement affecting employment.
There is no legal requirement to prevent workers accepting employment that is involved in a dispute and none that prevents employers from hiring such workers. Thus there would be no legal status for commission refusal to refer workers or accept employers' orders where the only reason for such action is that the employment is affected by a dispute. The commission would be in anything but a neutral position if it were to refuse to accept orders and refer workers since such action would favour the interests of the workers involved against those of the employer and indeed against the interest of other workers who are registered at the local office.
This policy is one that has been followed since the beginning of commission operations and one that has had wide acceptance. I am sure that you will appreciate that to change it would place the commission in a position where it could not act impartially and one that it could not defend on any legal grounds.

75. Departmental administration, $6,370,736. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, it is with a little apprehension that I take part today, for the first time, in the debate on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. During my few remarks, I shall probably not put forth very new ideas, but I shall at least have the opportunity of expressing my views.
When, in 1958, I was present for the first time at the debate on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, I was far from thinking that one day I would have the opportunity of taking part in it. I was probably mistaken in feeling, at the time, that to participate in such a debate, one
Supply-External Affairs had to be an expert on external affairs. I have changed my mind since, and I have realized that it is possible to learn something about external affairs by reading, and especially by listening to others who take part in such debates.
I had the opportunity in the last two years of being a delegate of our party on the joint Canada-U.S. parliamentary committee which, as you know, is composed of 24 members of the Canadian House of Commons and Senate and of 24 American senators and representatives. As a member of that committee, I had the opportunity, in Montreal and in Ottawa, for instance, to meet with members of the American committee and to form a friendship with them that will prove very useful, I think, and promote a better understanding of Canadian and American interests with regard to matters under consideration.
I also had the advantage, during the present session, of being a member of the same committee and to visit Washington, Omaha, Nebraska, and Colorado Springs, Colorado. We had the opportunity of meeting with the same American legislators and to renew our friendships.
Those trips are very instructive; those of us who go on them do not have to speak all the time and, besides, that is just what I did by applying the maxim: "Speech is silver, silence is golden."
I also had the privilege-and I thank the leader of my party for having selected me for that purpose-to attend the United Nations general assembly, in 1959, when I stayed in New York from November first until nearly the end of the meeting of the general assembly.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, in the United Nations, we meet people from almost all countries in the world, and there too we form solid friendships.
One thing which surprised me most agreeably at United Nations was the large share given over to French and to English at meetings of United Nations committees. I especially attended the meetings of the fourth committee, the trusteeship committee, where I noted that the French language, as well as the English language, was a diplomatic language par excellence.
In the course of the few minutes that will follow, I intend to deal more especially with those new peoples, those new African nations which, in recent days and particularly this year, have achieved either partial or total independence. I have acquired some

Supply-External Affairs familiarity with those things while attending the discussions of the fourth committee, and I was deeply interested in this question of Africa and of the independence of those countries peopled by the black race.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, in addition to those fully independent countries and countries under trusteeship-I refer particularly to Great Britain, France, Belgium, Italy and others I need not mention-there are also territories which lack a government of their own and are, in fact, only colonies or territories settled by other countries.
This year there have been remarkable changes in Africa. World opinion, it might be said, has been stirred by those countries. In 1960 they decided-and this I repeat with special emphasis-to take the leap from colonialism to independence. The people of Canada, whether French speaking or English speaking, or even of other ethnic groups, have lived through such periods in the past, although there was less agitation here in North America than there is in Africa at the present time. This country has slowly but surely developed from the colonial system to the complete independence we know today. Those African countries are perhaps passing more rapidly from the colonial system to freedom or independence, and that may be why they are meeting with greater difficulties. But we must not view with disfavour the rapid rise of those African people towards independence, and their wish to attain it more quickly, nor must we ignore the situation. Not only must we not disapprove their attitude, but we must realize that they are right and that it is up to us to help them. I am happy to note that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), stated yesterday, if I understood rightly, that the policy of Canada was to help those countries attain their independence by all possible means.
At this stage of my remarks, Mr. Chairman,
I want to voice a criticism which, I hope, is a constructive one, and which is directed both to the present government and to the former, which I did not have the honour to support in this house but whose virtues I have proclaimed in my riding and in my province.
Whenever, at meetings of the fourth committee of the United Nations, or of the trusteeship council, there was discussion on proposals submitted by member states, and more particularly by Asian countries, to accelerate the attainment of independence by those African countries, such as the Cam-eroons, Nyasaland and others, I believe that it was generally the policy of Canada to abstain from voting.
[Mr. Roberge.)
I know that there were such abstentions at the time when the external affairs policy was decided by the Liberal administration, but I think it was a mistake.
It is true that, at the time, the trend of those countries towards independence was perhaps less marked than today, but this mild reproach which I am now addressing to those who were then managing the affairs of our country, is also meant for those who are doing so now; indeed, I have noticed that more often than not, and, too often in the last year, in my opinion, Canada failed to take an official stand when those African countries were clamouring for their independence.
There probably was a good reason for taking such a stand, and it is possible that Canada was more inclined to make its influence felt behind the scenes than to do so officially, by casting a vote. However, those countries are looking to Canada, and their people know that Canada has no territorial economic or commercial ambitions with regard to their countries.
Of course, Canada would gladly trade with them, but such is not the ultimate purpose of Canada's policy. Canada's aim is to enable the peoples of Africa to live at last as we do here in Canada, and when I say live, Mr. Chairman, I do not mean our way of life but our standard of living.
I made some study of the situation in those countries, especially of a table published in Le Devoir of December 24, 1959, which had published several articles on the international situation with respect to countries of Africa.
I noted that some of the countries of Africa are very large in area, and that others are smaller. I also noted that those countries that are now independent, or will be so later this year or in the future, are linked about equally with the two large groups in the civilized world. Eighteen are in some way or other linked with France, through bonds of friendship, or by political or cultural ties.
Sixteen are linked with the United Kingdom by identical ties; three are linked with Italy, two with Belgium, two with Spain, three with Portugal, one with South Africa and one with the United States.
On the whole, we find that those countries are divided about equally between the Latin or French culture and the Anglo-Saxon culture.

A study of this table leads to the conclusion that Canada, being bilingual, will have a specific part to play with regard to those English or French speaking nations.
And so, what should Canada do to help those countries?
On that same day, Le Devoir published an article signed by Msgr. Marcel Lefebvre, archbishop of Dakar, under the following heading:
The duty of Christian states towards new Africa.
This article had the following subhead:
Warning to the West.
The attitude of countries which, in spite of many reservations, have retained Christian civilization as the basis for private, public, national and international law, should be unanimous:	they
should support those governments which have adopted, as the basis for their constitution, those principles which safeguard man's spiritualistic nature and, therefore, his fundamental freedoms.
This distinguished churchman refers to the part that Canada could play. I quote:
Canada, and particularly French speaking Canada, could play a leading part in building up those new African states.
There is no doubt, as I have indicated, that those nations are looking our way. They possibly do not ask us for directives with respect to their international or internal policies, but they certainly expect our moral and even material support. Thus they could hope to achieve not only political independence, but also spiritual, industrial and commercial independence.
Mr. Chairman, if we really believe in the intrinsic value of our way of life, in Canada or in western countries, it is our duty to protect it, and not by forcing our views upon other countries, but by showing them that we are right.
I do not want to take issue with the attitude taken by my colleague from Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin). The solution he suggests is perhaps the best. Personally, however-and I repeat this-I say that if we really believe in the value of our way of life, let us protect it and let us act in such a way that others may benefit from it.
At the beginning of my remarks, I dealt with the Canada-United States parliamentary group of which I was a member. I had the honour to meet one of the American legislators, Senator Frank Church, of Idaho, who this very week made the opening speech at the Democratic convention just held in the United States.
Here is what the senator said Mr. Chairman, according to the New York Times of Tuesday, July 12, 1960:
Supply-External Affairs
(Text):
We live on a shrunken planet where the prevailing order of the past three centuries has been destroyed. New nations rise from the wreckage of old empires, so that our world, like ancient Gaul, lies divided in three parts; one part consists of the western countries led by the United States; one part of the communist countries dominated by the Soviet union; and the third part of the newly emerging nations in the old colonial areas of Africa, Asia, and the southern seas.
These underdeveloped and uncommitted countries constitute the "no-man's lands" on which the fate of the human race will be determined.
(Translation):
A little farther on he stated:
(Text):
Two ways of life-communism and freedom- are thus locked in a mortal competition. Until the debris from the broken summit conference in Paris has been cleared, until the tumult that turned the president back from Tokyo has been better understood, we cannot know for sure what form this competition will take. But this we do know. We will either win it or lose it. There is no way out of it.
(Translation):
A moment ago, I was asking what attitude bilingual Canada should take towards those countries. One way of helping those African countries would be to establish frequent contacts with their national leaders; visits by high officials, ministers and members; exchange of personnel, either French speaking or English speaking.
That is what is being done in the case of Ceylon and Israel, and other countries whose names I forget. The commonwealth affords opportunities for such contacts, regardless of the colour of the peoples concerned.
In my opinion, the field in which Canada should take the lead would be in countries that are not yet part of the commonwealth or of the French community. Those countries are completely independent. It is with such countries, more than anywhere else, that exchanges of personnel should take place, at the university level. Graduates of Canadian universities could be sent out there to teach, while those Africans could come here to supplement their training.
In the administrative field, our assistance would no doubt be appreciated. It would not be a matter of imposing on them an administrative machinery identical with our own, but one which, firmly established, would meet with their principles and their needs. The most direct way would be to exchange officials at either the federal or the provincial level.

Mr. Chairman, I think the objectives of our foreign policy are agreed upon. We hope Canada can make its full contribution toward the maintenance of the peace of the world, toward improving the economic standards of people everywhere, and toward increasing freedom for all mankind. Within that framework I think we are all agreed.
I listened very carefully yesterday to the speech delivered by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and in connection with the disarmament negotiations and in connection with the experience in attempting to improve consultations at NATO the minister was quite comprehensive and frank. There are certain aspects of the disarmament talks that I wish he might have elaborated on somewhat further: for instance, the concrete

proposals that Canada put forward, and whether we took any decided independent initiative or whether in the main we copied ideas already put forward by others and then put them forward as our own proposals. However, Mr. Chairman, I really do not want to deal so much with what the minister said as with some of the things that were not said or dealt with in his speech.
There are many grave threats to peace in the world today; there are many grave situations. One of them is the situation in Cuba and Cuba's relations with other nations in the world. I think the Cuban situation is a powder keg that could explode at any time; yet there was not a single word in the minister's statement having to do with this most urgent question. I had expected that that kind of statement would be embodied in the minister's speech, because on July 11 I asked him a question on the situation in Cuba to which the minister replied as follows, as reported at page 6017 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows we have an ambassador in Cuba, so we are being kept informed of the situation. The answer of the minister was as follows:

It would seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that the minister might have included some discussion of this subject in his talk, because he ranged far afield; he went into many aspects of Canada's foreign policy, and he congratulated-I am not criticizing him for this; I associate myself with him-the people

Before I go into those subjects I should like to express the appreciation of both myself and my constituents of the fine work being done for Canada in the field of foreign policy by that great Canadian, our Secretary of State for External Affairs. Three years ago when we were on the hustings I would frequently be asked at public meetings, "If you people came to power who would be your foreign secretary?" I would say "The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, Mr. Howard C. Green". I said that he would be a great secretary of state for external affairs, a prophecy which has been borne out by events.
In recent months there has grown up in this country what I would call a campaign for neutralism. Unlike many campaigns this is not a co-ordinated effort, but the activities of many organizations and groups and individuals have given the impression that a large number of Canadians is in favour of Canada assuming a neutral role in world affairs. I think in fact this is a very small number, but those who are engaged in this campaign have been given a lot of attention.
I think one reason is that the dissenters are usually more newsworthy than those who support existing and traditional policies. Another reason is that the policies we have followed do not seem to have relieved the threat of war. The newspapers and magazines have played up other proposals which some people thought might be more successful.
The campaign for neutralism is supported in whole or in part by people of greatly different interests and political views. It is spurred on, of course, by the communists and fellow travellers associated with the Canadian peace congress which had its annual rally in Massey hall in Toronto on February 7 of this year. The president of this congress, Mr. James Endicott, had some astonishing things to say that night, including the following:
I believe that our movement fulfils the righteous purposes of God in history and that God uses the communists for the establishment of peace, whether they know it or not.
He also argued that Canada should withdraw from NATO and NORAD and proclaim its neutrality. It is not surprising to find this kind of thing coming from the Canadian peace congress, but it is very disturbing to find the proposal that we should withdraw from NORAD coming from quite a different body, the committee on nuclear disarmament at the University of Toronto. On page 16 of this committee's brief to the Prime Minister is this recommendation:
The committee therefore recommends that Canada should abrogate the NORAD agreement, making it quite clear that, in so doing, Canada's intention is not to cease co-operation with the United States


in matters of North American defence, but rather to regain its freedom to determine those policies within the framework of which it will co-operate.
This recommendation is made because the committee thinks Canada is permanently subordinated to the United States in the matter of North American defence.
Another voice which speaks in favour of a break with the United States is that of people who think if a war came it would be fought by Washington and the Kremlin, and that Canada would have no part in offence or defence. Since we are destined only to be a victim, why should we have any part in the defence preparations?
Still another group takes the position that by becoming neutral Canada could become the arbitrator between the United States and Russia. This group has become noisier since the U-2 was shot down over Russia. The Americans have been accused of taking unnecessary risks and of fumbling when they are caught. Canada is invited to stand between these adversaries and say "a plague on both your houses". Typical of this argument is the statement of a Toronto rabbi, Rabbi Abraham Feinberg, writing in the Toronto Globe and Mail on June 4, as follows:
I for one am not content to let the future of mankind and my children be decided by the blundering incompetence of the striped-pants brigade and military brass in Washington, or by the blustering hyprocisy of a diabolically shrewd and ruthless cabal in the Kremlin.
I think it must be said, Mr. Speaker, that while some of the promoters of neutralism are sincere people, most are status-seekers looking for an audience or acclaim. A recent book by an American commentator, Mr. James M. Minifie, has become the bible for the neutralists. Some reviewers have pronounced this a book that every thoughtful Canadian should read. Well, all I can say, Mr. Speaker, is that if a thoughtful Canadian begins to read this book he will have picked up very few thoughts of any value by the time he gets to the end of it. The purpose of this book is to show that Canada could contribute more to the peace of the world by adopting a policy of neutrality in place of continuing its association with the United States under NORAD and with the western powers under NATO.
The NORAD agreement is described as a contract which makes Canadian air defence services subservient to the United States, with the result that Canada has become a satellite of the United States. The argument goes on that because of this satellite status, Canada cannot express at the United Nations views that differ from United State views, and when our statements are the same as

those made by the United States they do not have the force they would have if Canada had proclaimed neutrality.
The NATO principle, says this author, has been prostituted and betrayed. The organization is now set up exclusively for the defence of the United States, with bases established in other countries for the sole purpose of diluting an attack on America. According to this writer the Americans have promoted defence installations in Canada so that the warheads will be dropped on Canada before they reach the United States. He put it this way:	"Better Saskatchewan than North
Dakota; better Winnipeg than Chicago". By taking the road to neutralism it is said that Canada would attract the support of other middle powers and this new force would put the brakes on imperialism and aggression.
The essence of all these arguments, Mr. Speaker, is that since present policies do not seem to be reducing the possibilities of war, Canada should take on the role of a neutral peacemaker. Well, the simple fact that the neutralists do not see is that the western countries are now facing a political and economic offensive of terrible proportions, .guided by men with a philosophy which goes against all traditional western values. We are all in the same boat. This is a time for unity and co-operation, not for petty dissent.
We all have some idea of the Russian and Chinese military strength. In 15 years the communists have taken over a dozen countries. We have been surprised and shocked by the Russian successes in space. We are bewildered by the recent tirades of Mr. Khrushchev, which are quite out of tune with his line of the past two years in favour of peaceful coexistence. But if you go back to Marx and Lenin and Stalin, the political manoeuvres should not be surprising. The communist goal is to dominate the world by using economic means, and war if necessary. This fact is frequently brought home to us by our own Prime Minister, who has said many times that while the tactics may be changed from time to time, the goal is the same.
I think this is a very good time for us to take another look at this definition of communist aims and the tactics they are prepared to adopt to reach their objectives. The objectives of the communist party were well expressed by Dmitri Manuilski, who in 1931 said in the Lenin school of political warfare:
War to the hilt between communism and capitalism is inevitable. Today, of course, we are not strong enough to attack. Our time will come in 20 or 30 years. The bourgeoisie will have to be put to sleep, so we will begin by launching the most spectacular peace movement on record. There
Supply-External Affairs
will be electrifying overtones and unheard-of concessions. The capitalist countries, stupid and decadent, will rejoice and co-operate in their own destruction. They will leap at another chance to be friends. As soon as their guard is down we shall smash them with our clenched fists.
The time has come for closer co-operation, not neutralism; closer co-operation in politics, in military planning and in trade. Americans are our best friends, and the fact is that United States military strength is now the only deterrent to further military adventures on the part of the communists and perhaps the only deterrent to a third world war.
In the defence efforts of the west, Canada must do her share in providing conventional arms and in helping to equip Canadian and American and western European forces. We must continue to hold to the principle that defence of the North American continent is indivisible. We must continue to make it clear that in the ideological struggle we are proud to stand up and be counted with the Americans.
I think however, we can do more than this. I believe we have to show the people in Asia and Africa that we sincerely care for them. We have to recruit foreign service officers who are prepared to spend their lives in those countries. We have to be prepared to make great increases in our grants of economic aid, and I shall have more to say on this point in a few moments. Here again we must find Canadians who will go abroad and live for long periods while the Canadian projects are brought to fruition. We must support the work of raising the standards of literacy in these countries and making available the results of our research.
Most important, we must get to work on these things immediately. There is too much talk about a national purpose and an international policy. What is needed is concrete and immediate action. Since Canada cannot be a major military power, I think we should give greater attention to helping to build a peaceful world by assisting less developed countries.
In a recently issued pamphlet Paul G. Hoffman, director of the United Nations special fund, has pointed out that 1J billion people in 100 countries in the world are by any standard terribly poor. He points out that, apart from political and moral considerations, the western countries should be concerned with this problem. If the per capita income of these people could be raised by only 1 per cent a year over the coming 10 years, they could offer to the United States alone a market for an estimated $14 billion of its exports in 1970.
These nations, he says, have become a great new economic frontier. He points out

Supply-External Affairs that the aid programs of the fifties in terms of improved living standards have not been very impressive. In these 100 countries the average per capita income in 1950 was approximately $90. Probably it reached slightly over $100 per person in 1959. The gross income grew at the rate of 3 per cent a year, but because the population of these countries increased in this decade by 200 million people, the net increase in income per person was only about 1 per cent or $1 a year.
Hoffman's objective is that the western countries assist the people of these underdeveloped areas so that the annual growth of the per capita income is increased from 1 per cent to 2 per cent each year for the next 10 years. This would raise the present level of about $100 per capita per year to approximately $125. He points out that one important part of the work is in the surveying of natural resources and in training people in the less developed areas in the skills they must develop so that they can make good use of their natural resources.
In a 10-year period the less developed countries should be able to earn around $378 billion through the sale of their goods in world markets. He goes on to say that a reasonable estimate of the total in the decade for these countries, if they are to double the per capita rate of economic growth, is about $440 billion, which means that some $62 billion in investment capital will be required in addition to estimated earnings from exports or, on the average, about $6.2 billion a year. He says that an additional $8 billion at least over the 10 years might be required to cover other costs, such as debts, service charges, transportation charges and other services.
A total of $70 billion would thus seem to be needed, or about $7 billion a year. This is about $3 billion more than flowed to the less developed areas in 195758. To make up this $3 billion a year, increased private investment and bankable loans might account for about $1 billion a year, leaving $2 billion a year, or $20 billion over the decade, which will have to be raised through other means. Repayment of many of the loans that must be made should not overburden the economies of these countries; they must be for long terms at low rates of interest with the beginning dates of repayment of principal deferred. Hoffman hopes that at least half of the $20 billion needed for the coming decade may be channelled through the proposed international development association, or $10 billion over the period or $1 billion a year.

All of us supported the bill recently brought before the house relating to Canada's participation in the newly established international development association, and I think we would all associate ourselves with what was said in that connection in this chamber by the hon. member for Essex East, that this measure was perhaps among the most important proposals the Minister of Finance has laid before this house.
In addition to the moneys that may be provided by way of loans through the international development association we can, of course, look forward to the continued use of the facilities of the international bank for reconstruction and development and to the continued use of the international monetary fund.
Canada, of course, will continue to support in a financial way and by providing technical assistance the agencies of the United Nations engaged in assisting these areas in the matter of surveys, fiscal policy, public administration, industrial development and in other fields as well. It seems to me that we are moving much too slowly in this field, however. According to the best informed opinion, that of Mr. Hoffman, some $10 billion will be required over the next 10 years from the international development association, yet the total subscription to this fund is $1 billion.
As far as we could ascertain at the time the bill which had to do with Canada's participation in the fund was before us, no specific plans have yet been made for the use of the subscriptions to that association, and it appears that for the time being at least there are no plans for increasing the total subscriptions. So here we are providing a fund which seems to have a total anticipated subscribed amount of $1 billion, while the best expert in the world in this field says that this sum of money could be used effectively and absorbed to advantage in the very first year. I believe that Canada has a great opportunity and obligation to increase its assistance in these fields, even if it means greater sacrifices on the part of the Canadian people imposed by taxation.
I must say that when I read the results of the private campaign carried out for world refugee year I get very discouraged about the proposition that very much can be done by voluntary activity having regard to the greatness of world problems. If we are going to go into economic and other aid to less fortunate people in a large way it seems to me the initiative has to come from the government and the funds have to be taxed out of the people.

Having regard to our population, perhaps no country in the world has a greater reservoir of trained engineers, economists and experts in farming, soil conservation and land use. Tremendous benefits have already been brought about by Canada's Colombo plan projects. Earlier this week I had the opportunity of discussing those projects with a young man in my constituency, Mr. Keith Spicer, who under the sponsorship of the Canada Council recently travelled abroad to inspect those undertakings. I wish hon. members could have heard that discussion and seen the enthusiasm and sense of pride which shone in the face of that young man when he talked about the good will which is being built up for this country in India, Pakistan and Ceylon, and when he talked about the tangible material advantages which he had seen coming to those countries as a result of the efforts of the government of Canada and of our administrators and technicians who are associated with those projects. It was stimulating to see the excitement which this plan had aroused in this eminently qualified young Canadian.
I should like to suggest to the minister that the government give consideration to a project which has been talked about for some time and most recently at last year's Couchiching conference; that next year the government send a team of 100 student volunteers to those Colombo plan projects which are under the oversight of the Canadian authorities, and that those students be paid their fares and a subsistence allowance while working abroad. I suggest that those be people who have finished their third or fourth year at university, people who have a genuine desire to serve their fellow men and who have some real knowledge of the countries to which they will be going. I think the group should be made up of students in social work, teaching, engineering and medicine, and that they should be prepared to take on any useful work which might be assigned to them by the full time administrators.
To finance such a program for a year would cost only $200,000, or perhaps something less than that, certainly less than one half of one per cent of Canada's annual appropriation for the Colombo plan. Not only would the assisted countries greatly benefit, but Canada would obtain the benefit of having a group of young people who had some real knowledge of the problems of the people in those countries.
I do not think we should be pessimistic about the influence that Canada can have in those Asian countries. Anyone who goes to a university campus these days finds dozens of students who are looking around in a
Supply-External Affairs serious way for a chance to serve their country and the world. It is our obligation, I believe, as members of parliament to provide leadership by presenting specific programs to the government, and 1 submit it is the duty of the government not to miss this great opportunity.

Mr. Chairman, in rising even at this inconvenient and hungry hour to participate in this debate, may I begin by joining in the tribute which the minister has paid to his department, to the men and women in it who work, as the minister said, with industry, intelligence and complete loyalty to their minister. May I also echo what has been said on this side in appreciation of the sincerity and devotion of the minister as he faces many difficult, complicated and sometimes dangerous problems. If we criticize him, as we do, and as we will, and as he used to criticize us, it is not without the recognition that our criticism should be constructive and that we should always realize that we are criticizing foreign policy, which is something on which we should all do our best to be united.
The debate seems to me to have been carried along in a very constructive line. I think the minister will agree with me when I say there have been some useful ideas put forward by members on all sides of the house which we hope may be helpful to the minister as he faces the problems that confront him and the government of the day in this field.
The foreign policy of a country can, I suppose, be divided as Gaul was divided, into three parts; into principles, into policies, into procedures or perhaps I should say purposes, policies and procedures. So far as purposes are concerned, as has already been pointed out in this debate, there is no difference among us all. Our purposes are the same; as are the purposes of the Canadian people, namely to carry on foreign policy in a way which may make a contribution to peace and security in a dangerous, turbulent and uneasy world. Our policies should be, as I have just stated, as united as they can be made to be. Of course that does not mean that when we on this side disagree with a particular policy we will not express that disagreement. However, we should certainly try to keep those disagreements to a minimum.
We will criticize the procedures, as we have, whenever we think those procedures are not best for the purpose of implementing the policy. If in our speeches in a debate such as this we criticize the government, and if we criticize the policies of our friends and allies and do not spend all our time

Supply-External Affairs criticizing the policies of our potential enemies, I hope we shall not be accused of following the communist propaganda line. It is just as absurd to make the suggestion that because of a speech which may be critical of our government or of our friends, we are indulging in communist propaganda, as it would have been for us on this side to criticize the minister on the same score because when he came back from Paris last December, in times which were more cheerful and when there were more grounds for optimism, he said:
The time has come for the west to accept Russian protestations of sincerity at face value in order to find a way to end the armaments race.
Or when he said, and I quote from the press:
Our view is that we have to accept the honesty of Russian intentions in this committee.
He was referring to the disarmament committee. The minister made that statement in good faith, and it would be very unfair, indeed slanderous, to the minister to suggest that he was following communist propaganda or was weakening the democratic line by making that kind of statement.
So, Mr. Chairman, while I am on this matter, perhaps in a debate like this I can dispose of my own attitude toward communist policies by saying that those policies today, far more than a year ago, constitute a threat to peace, just as their principles are deadly to freedom and everything we stand for. The news that has just come in this morning of the threatened, or possible, or indicated desire of the Soviet leader to intervene in the Congo is just another indication of the dangerous character of communist policy over the years. We have to accept that fact. Perhaps we should speak a little more about that danger because there always is the danger of taking it for granted. Their policies are dangerous and their principles are deadly. If I do not keep repeating that in debates on foreign affairs it does not mean that I am unaware of it.
As I have just said, Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that the situation is more serious than it was nor is that seriousness to be assessed in the light of the tribal rituals and the exuberant vitality of United States political conventions; nor is it reflected in the happy holiday North American atmosphere of the summer of 1960. All we have to do to appreciate how serious the position is-I am not being panicky or unduly pessimistic; I am talking about seriousness-is to look around us in the world at what has happened in the last two or three months. In Turkey, a NATO country, the government was forced out of office by violence. I am not saying this in either any critical or approving sense,


but in that country a friendly NATO government was forced out of office by violence. In Korea unease and riots resulted in a change of government. Perhaps it was overdue, but the way it was brought about creates anxiety. Violence in Japan was carried to the point where the President of the United States could not visit that allied country in the Pacific. In Tibet fighting is still being carried on by those who are supposed to be grateful for the liberation they have had through the instrumentality of the Chinese communists; but who are so little impressed by that liberation that a year afterward they are still fighting against the whole communist might of Peking.
Then there is the Congo. Mention of the Congo gives me an opportunity to Tinderline what the hon. member for Assiniboia said; that while we were very interested in and appreciated the statement the minister gave us in his tour d'horizon, there were some omissions. Perhaps the minister will fill in some of those omissions when he replies to all the questions that have been brought up; because of course, as one who has occupied his position, I know it is not possible in an introductory statement to cover every part of the world and every problem in the world.
The Congo is worth pretty close examination, as a country where independence and anarchy came almost simultaneously. This indicates that the African winds of chance, as Right Hon. Harold Macmillan has designated them, are blowing with hurricane force. Then there is Cuba, on which the hon. member for Assiniboia dwelt and I think quite rightly. This is a danger, and a difficulty, much closer to home, where the excitable violence of a revolutionary government has produced in the United States, because of the way it expresses itself, a far greater reaction than did the despotic tyranny that preceded it and which was at least in part responsible for the present violence. The pendulum swings, and if you have an extreme on the one side you are almost bound to have an extreme on the other side.
I think the United States of America has shown very great patience in this situation up to the present time against very considerable provocation, I suggest that the United States will have to show even more patience, and that is not going to be easy in the light of what is going on on the island of Cuba. Intervention by armed forces or intervention by forces of any kind, the illegal use of force to protect even vital economic and other interests, is not now possible in the world in which we live. The Suez incident certainly showed that, and the United States should be just about the first country in the world

to draw the right conclusions from that incident. The same principles that were applied by those who believed in them, and I was one, regarding United Nations intervention in the Suez would have to be applied to the western hemisphere in the same circumstances.
While the United States government has, as I have emphasized, shown real patience in the face of much provocation, that is why I think the President's reference to the application of the Monroe doctrine, in the terms in which he made that reference, was rather hasty; I mean the application of the Monroe doctrine to prevent any communist state emerging in the western hemisphere. I think it would have been better in all respects if the President, if he felt it necessary to issue that warning, should have done so in terms of inter-American conventions, two of which have dealt with this matter, the Rio treaty of 1947 against aggression, and not only military aggression in its terms, and the Caracas resolution of 1956.

1954. I also think the announcement at this particular moment in Washington of a new plan for economic assistance to Latin American states, desirable as that is in itself, was bad timing. I have read in the New York Times that when it was announced someone designated as a senior, experienced Latin American diplomat commented in Washington that it was a fine thing. He said that the Latin American states would appreciate it very much, but he thought they would probably give more credit for it to Castro than to President Eisenhower.
All this turmoil fairly close to home cannot help but raise some anxious thoughts in our minds, especially as we know that in this area as in other areas of the world, and I have mentioned some of them, international communism, the international communist conspiracy, is ready, anxious and happy to fish in all these troubled waters, to catch what it can in Korea, Japan, the Congo or Cuba. Communism may not be in itself the origin of all these difficulties and dangers and uprisings, but communism is always there to take advantage of them.
This is a very brief survey, but I think it does help to show what we are up against in this summer of 1960 and perhaps underlines the desirability of the western governments, the leaders of the western world, and all of us, showing a more sober realization of the deterioration of the situation in the last six months than has sometimes been the case. That does not mean, as I see it, panic or provocation or despair or anything like 79951-0-401
Supply-External Affairs that, but surely it does mean the necessity for strong, consistent, steady, determined and persistent leadership, especially in Washington where the centre of western power lies and from the consequences of whose decisions none of us can isolate ourselves. Surely in the next few months it requires, even more than ever, a really effective, steady and continuous direction of policy in Washington, not only strictly United States policy alone but United States policy in its coalition aspects, too. In that regard it is far more important to keep driving down the middle of the international political fairways than it is to improve our golf scores.
I recall during the blitz in London, one morning after a particularly noisy and destructive evening prior to a week end, taking off to escape from the sleepless night to my suburban golf course. As I was about to drive off from the first tee my caddy, who was a friend of mine whom I had used for some time, said, "Mr. Pearson, please try not to slice this time; please try to keep on the fairway, because there are unexploded bombs in the rough". Well, today the unexploded bombs on the international fairways are not all in the rough; they are right on the fairways, and it is important that we should do everything we can to harmlessly detonate them.
The main responsibility for this lies, as it has, because of the circumstances of its power, in the United States. The main responsibility for leadership lies in Washington at a time when the unity of the coalition is as essential, if not more essential, than it has been at any time since the end of world war II. We would be making a great mistake if we were to rely too much on Mr. Khrushchev's crude brutality, his transparent efforts to divide us, as a means of keeping us together. This perhaps is the lesson to be drawn from some of the incidents of the last couple of months. I hope the minister and the committee will not think I am too egotistical if I quote from an article of mine which I wrote for a magazine called Foreign Affairs. I said this:
The Immediate effect of Khrushchev's crude behaviour in Paris; of his sudden torpedoing of the conference for which he bore so much responsibility in the first place; of his insulting attempt to humiliate the President by presenting him with demands which he knew would be entirely unacceptable-the immediate effect of all this was to bring the members of the alliance closer together. That was the inevitable and the right reaction.
Then I went on:
But let us not draw wrong, if comforting, conclusions from this first reaction. The U-2 incident and, even more, the way it was handled in Washington, have caused some anxious questioning in other friendly capitals, not about the aims of United States policy so much as about the methods used in pursuing those aims, both in defence and

Then I ended by saying:
If some damage has been done to United States leadership within the coalition, that can be and, we hope, soon will be repaired. This, however, must be more than a patching job, more than the comforting words of a communique. Otherwise there will be another crisis-
Perhaps we have one.
_which will expose other weaknesses inside our
coalition and which will require other remedies. We cannot afford this kind of erosion which, the communists hope, will eventually lead to the disintegration of our alliance. If the Atlantic coalition is to survive, it must reduce these centrifugal disturbances to a minimum, through sure, confident and wise leadership and with continuous and far closer consultation among its members than previously, in order to work out a common policy in the face of a common threat.
This was in connection with what is known as the U-2 episode. We have had another one since then. A United States plane was shot down either over or off the Russian coast. I do not believe we should take the Russian version of this incident as the truth. We have learned, surely, from experience that most of their statements in a situation of this kind are false. However, I believe we have a right to ask ourselves, whether that plane was flying over Russian territory or territorial waters or adjacent to them, what are planes of this kind doing in those areas, close to that country, in times of tension, fear and disturbances. The hon. member for Assiniboia has already mentioned this matter.
If the work being carried on by these air force planes in this area is purely nonmilitary, scientific and peaceful, surely it could be made known before they initiated the operation and publicity could be given to what they are doing out over the open seas. If that is not the case then certainly the allies of the country concerned, in this case the United States, and especially those allies who have bases from which these planes can fly, have a right to know what is being done before it is being done. There is a real danger in this kind of incident in the circumstances of today.
The London Times of July 13 had an editorial on this incident, and perhaps I may be permitted to quote one or two sentences from it because I think they are very pertinent. The Times says:
The Russians are inherently suspicious-
Of course that is true and it has been true for centuries.
These suspicions are not immaterial. Wars have not always started because something had actually happened. It can be enough for a powerful country's leaders to believe they have. Steps can then be taken with consequences that are irretrievable ...


incidents are the symptoms, but not the causes of tension. They will go on, in one form or another, until the tension is eased. At the same time, any one of them may cause it to snap.
Well, we know what the snapping of tension might lead to today. I think perhaps the minister, when he replies, should tell us in so far as security considerations permit-we have no right to ask him to go further in this or any other matter-what is the Canadian position with regard to Canadian air fields and bases which are, quite rightly, open to United States use as a member of the coalition. Are we satisfied that these bases cannot be used in a way which would leave us open to a charge of participating in an operation because of the use of Canadian bases, which could be characterized as unfriendly or, worse, as aggressive by the Soviet union or any other communist country? I am not suggesting that these charges would be accurate. I am suggesting we ought to know what the position is, both with regard to the arrangements that may or may not exist and with regard to any other arrangements, to make sure that we know what is going on in respect of every plane that flies off a Canadian airfield.
Now, Mr. Chairman, surely we should examine the situation inside our coalition in the light of the deterioration of the international situation, in the light of the collapse of the summit and the depressing events elsewhere, some of which I have ventured to mention. The London Economist of May 28 contained this paragraph about the necessity for such re-examination:
The full extent of the dangers inherent in the Paris break-down is only beginning to penetrate the public consciousness. After all, the sky has not fallen. It can only be said that the best way to remove the danger is not to pretend that it does not exist, and not to imagine that the posture of military readiness is the sole preventive of war that the wit of man can devise. In the west we need to be frank with ourselves, besides being true to our obligations to each other.
One result of this reassessment which has taken place, and I am sure it has taken place in the Canadian government as in other governments, has been a re-examination of the value of summit diplomacy. There are times when diplomacy at the heights, on the summit, by the top men of the world can be useful and valuable. There have been occasions in history where it has been indispensable. Summit diplomacy is not new; it goes back as far as history goes back. Even today summit diplomacy can be helpful in meetings of leaders of states, small informal meetings, as small and as informal as possible. But summit diplomacy, as we have learned from the collapse of the last two or three months, can be dangerous as well as valuable.

I have stated those dangers as I saw them many times during the last two or three years. Most of them result from the exaggerated optimism which is created by the build-up before the meetings; because being summit meetings they cannot be permitted to fail, at least for propaganda purposes, before they are held. This exaggerated optimism before the meeting, which is not fulfilled by the results of the meeting, is usually followed by exaggerated disillusionment, exaggerated pessimism and excitable uncertainty. And that means that if we are to have summit diplomacy it is essential to have careful preparation. Perhaps that is not very easy at the present time, when you are dealing with communist states.
So I think it would be a good thing, and I said this long before the collapse on the last summit, if we could get back to the ordinary channels of diplomacy, back to conventional and direct diplomacy where governments can work things out without there being 2,000 newspaper men in the corridors, if you could get 2,000 newspaper men in a corridor, or without having 150 cameras in the room. We should also get back to the United Nations itself as a channel for negotiation and diplomacy.
It has been pointed out by more than one speaker in this debate, although we all know how invaluable and indispensable the United Nations is, that it is not in its present form a suitable agency for general security. It is not a world government or a world power. It does not govern; it has no power behind its recommendations; and it has no law behind them either. However, it can provide and it has provided a good channel, a good forum for diplomacy and negotiation. And it has done, in certain circumstances, some very useful work in this regard which we are often inclined to forget about.
I do not mean that we can use the full assembly of the United Nations for this purpose; of course we cannot. By 1962 the assembly of the United Nations, according to what I read the other day, especially because of the emergence of new states mostly in Africa, will perhaps consist of 100 members. In that group of 100 there will perhaps be 40 or 50 new states without much experience, some without the resources of other and older states for the conduct of diplomacy, some of them indeed without very much in the way of resources at all. But all will be proud and jealous and determined to assert themselves, as they will, at the United Nations assembly. In this 100 there may be 30 or 33 from Africa, and that will be a terrific strain on the organization, even for 79951-0-4011
Supply-External Affairs debate. So it is idle to think we can use this kind of assembly machinery for purposes of negotiation.
This does not mean that we cannot use other parts of the United Nations or that we cannot modify the existing machinery, even though that would require an amendment to the charter and you would run up against the veto. Outside the house a few months ago, when talking about the United Nations as a channel for diplomacy, I said:
The assembly, as it approaches its century in membership, should become more and more a forum for the debating and the declaration of great principles for the condemnation of action which contravenes these principles, and for setting up and supervising smaller bodies for specific tasks, such as disarmament.
We also need a smaller body in continuous session for the negotiation of political questions. For this the security council could enlarge its membership, perhaps double it, although that would require an amendment to the charter. Here in this enlarged membership Asian and African countries could be more adequately represented; and this enlarged council, meeting more often than at present, could deal with many of the political questions on a week to week basis which are now reserved for the assembly each year.
A body of this type, really a little assembly, would compensate for some of the weaknesses of the increasingly unwieldy larger assembly without interfering with the functions of the security council, which the veto and the cold war have frustrated in any event. However, it can be done, and surely it is desirable to press with all the vigour we can for the greater use of the United Nations in the search for solutions to the dangerous problems which confront us.
If it is impossible in this search, as it might well be, indeed perhaps as it has been to some extent in recent years, to persuade the great powers, the powers with world responsibilities and world interests, to work in the way I have suggested through the United Nations, why should we not use the middle powers as a group far more than we have? This idea has already been expressed in this debate by more than one speaker.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres suggested last night that we should put aside the two great super powers and collect all the powers in between, irrespective of their forms of government, and see if we could not work out solutions by conferences of that kind. That is a very interesting idea, I suspect, indeed the hon. member indicated himself, that it would not be too easy to work out because if you put the two super powers on one side you might still have 98

But as it is becoming more and more desirable I think it would be possible to get a working group of middle powers, powers with responsibility and without world interests or world power, but with enough power to discharge their responsibilities. Perhaps Canada could take the intiative here and become one of the leaders of a group of such powers, powers determined to take new initiatives, to make new attempts as a group to ease tension, and to promote disarmament and widen the areas of cooperation.
If I were asked what were the concrete initiatives which such a group might be taking at the forthcoming United Nations assembly, or the one after that, I can think of a few things. I have mentioned them before and the minister has no doubt considered them, but I would like to put them on record because when you make these general statements it is useful to try to follow them up, if you can, with some concrete proposals.
One of the things which should be done and which should be pressed, I think, is that the Secretary General of the United Nations should be present or represented at every international meeting, summit or otherwise, which is held outside the United Nations. I do not know whether all meetings in question would accept the Secretary General of the United Nations as a representative at an international conference, but I think the more we could do to establish the idea that he should always be there, the better it would be.
I think also that consideration should be given again, because it has already been given by the government, to the middle powers I have talked about bringing up at the United Nations pending an international agreement the possibility of a self-denying ordinance under which all those powers of the world which do not now manufacture or use nuclear weapons will agree not to manufacture or not to use them.

I am asking the government if they have given this matter consideration. 1 mentioned this a year ago, or perhaps two years ago, and if the hon. gentleman will read Hansard he will see the terms in which I put it from this side of the house.
