speechtext: If the Leader of the Opposition does not mind my intervening, may I say that this is one of the most difficult problems Canada faces. Is it the policy of the party which the hon. gentleman leads that there should be no nuclear weapons used by Canadian forces or stored in Canada?

I have not said that. I have said that we should consider whether the middle powers, and some of them would be in NATO, should not consider the desirability in present circumstances of adopting what I called a self-denying ordinance against the manufacture of nuclear weapons-that is already, I believe, the policy of the government-and whether we should not consider the restriction of the use of nuclear weapons to those countries which now have them. This is exactly the kind of consideration which is being given to this problem by political parties in Great Britain and other NATO countries at the present time.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does the Leader of the Opposition not think that very policy is already contained in the resolution which was passed by the United Nations a year ago?
I do not think this policy is contained in any resolution that I know anything about.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: One was passed last year.
So much the better. If one was passed the minister will be able to put it on the record; and I say, let us follow it up.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am referring to the Irish resolution of last year.
I did not know the Irish resolution went as far as that, but if it did, and if we supported that resolution-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Everybody did.

If a resolution has been passed at the United Nations which everybody agreed to, it is probably not the kind of self-denying ordinance which I have in mind, because I have learned from experience that when a

resolution is passed unanimously it does not require much in terms of action, or policy or implementation.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh.

I qualify what I have said. Perhaps it requires even more in the way of implementation, but it is usually in such form that there is no obligation involved in it, that is if everybody, including the communist countries, accepted it.
There is a third proposal; that we should press ahead with the formation of a United Nations emergency force. I bring this up every time I speak on foreign affairs, and I make no apology for returning to the subject. The Minister of National Defence, speaking before the defence committee not long ago, as reported on page 198 of the record-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: On a question of order, I think that committee has not yet reported to the house and it is against the rules to quote from proceedings in a committee until a report has been submitted.

The minister is right; I should not quote from the report. I will put it this way. Members of the government have stated on more than one occasion that this government has recommended more than once the establishment of an international police force under the auspices of the United Nations. When the minister replies, perhaps he will give us some details as to when these recommendations were put forward and in what form.
Whether or not the Canadian government has made formal recommendation to this effect-and we shall learn about that-the situation which has confronted the world in the last two or three days with regard to the Congo underlines the desirability, perhaps even the necessity, of having some permanent stand-by force of this kind. I know that two years ago when this matter was brought up in the United Nations no progress was possible, and no progress has been made since that time.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is the Leader of the Opposition not aware that the secretary general is against that proposal?

Of course I am aware of that; I have talked with the secretary general about this matter, and I know his reasons for objecting. But I also know that it could be put forward in a way which would remove most of the objections held by the secretary general, just as I am aware that when this matter was put forward two years ago the proposal was first made by the United States. With all respect for the United States, when a proposal of this kind is put forward at the assembly by a great power, the U.S.S.R.,
Supply-External Affairs or the United States or France, it starts off very often with one or two strikes against it. I am suggesting that this matter could be pursued by the group of middle powers. One of the things they would want to do would be to discuss it with the secretary general in the light of the secretary general's objections to the proposals put forward in the past, of which I know something.
Another matter which would fall under consideration of this group of middle powers would be disarmament. My hon. friend from Essex East went into this in considerable detail yesterday and I do not propose to again traverse the ground he covered, I thought, so well and so wisely. There has been a certain disillusion at the collapse of the Geneva discussions. The minister himself said yesterday that some of his earlier optimism-and I am not quarrelling with him for displaying that optimism-has had to be modified in the light of events. That often happens to optimists, and it should not necessarily lead to despair. Perhaps it should lead to renewed determination to secure new grounds for optimism.
There is not very much ground for immediate optimism in the armament situation which confronts us at the present time, but there is no ground for excessive pessimism, either. We have been trying to deal with this disarmament problem ever since the end of the first world war, and I speak as one who has been concerned with just about every disarmament conference which took place at the United Nations until 1957, when I stopped attending those meetings. All the difficulties we face now and all the arguments for and against were encountered by those earlier disarmament committees.
One thing the recent collapse has shown is that you cannot dissociate policies from armament. As I think the hon. member for Saskatoon pointed out last night in a quotation from Sir Winston Churchill, if the state of the world were peaceful and tensions had begun to disappear we would not have these excessive and dangerous armaments. It is because the world is in a perilous condition that we have these heaped up armaments. The effort to reduce armaments, important as it is, can never be dissociated from the effort to ease tensions. Anyone who knew what was happening in the world in the last year or two knew that we had to have realism with our optimism as we faced this new disarmament committee set up a year ago by the United Nations.
I myself never felt that an agency for disarmament in which you had five communist states on one side of the table-unlike the Seigniory club conference-and five noncommunist states on the other side of the

Supply-External Affairs table in the atmosphere of today, had too much chance of success or of making progress. We had the same experience in the earlier committee of five, except that it was worse. In that case there was only one communist state against four non-communist states. The larger meeting was perhaps a little improvement on that. But this mechanism by which the two sides face each other across a table and hope to reduce tension and disarmament at the same time represents a forum for discussion which I think is not normally too effective for that purpose.
I wonder whether Canada could not perhaps suggest some other approach. The Prime Minister told Mr. Khrushchev that the Canadian government has adopted throughout in the 10-nation committee a strong and independent stand. My friend the hon. member for Essex East dealt with that independent stand yesterday. But if in fact we desire to adopt an independent stand, would it not be desirable to at least consider an entirely new approach?
I have mentioned this before outside the house. Would it not be desirable to adopt an entirely new approach by which this group of middle powers under United Nations authorization by resolution of the assembly, could set up a disarmament committee which would exclude all the permanent members of the council? I know the objection that would be raised-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The other people would have to disarm.

That is just what I was going to say. That is the objection that would be raised at once; it would exclude the people that should disarm. I am not suggesting that a committee of middle powers could draft a disarmament treaty and impose it on any one, because of course they could not; but when these great powers meet in disarmament committees, and when there is a middle power like Canada that has to work within the western five-and I am not criticizing this-we have learned that there is no possibility even for agreement on draft provisions of a treaty, let alone the figures.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I ask the Leader of the Opposition a question? Does the hon. gentleman have in mind, for example, including Czechoslovakia in that proposal?

I do not think you could include in that kind of group any country that got its orders directly and demonstrably from a great power, but there are countries in the United Nations which are not committed to one side or the other. There are some countries that are committed to the


western side; but Canada is one, we are told, that does not get its orders from any power, and rightly so. If we could draft the provisions of a treaty and then submit them to the United Nations and to the great powers, that might be a step forward. It might result in a lot of the preliminary work being done in a way that would be agreeable to a great majority of United Nations members, and which would make it more difficult later for the great powers to turn down provisions of this kind.
I ask the minister if that approach is not worth considering, and I put it on no higher plane than that. Perhaps after consideration it would be found impossible or impractical, but I should like to see it considered.
There is something else in this field, and that is the question of nuclear testing. Some progress has been made at Geneva, but we are not on the eve of an agreement as was hoped a few months ago. My friend the hon. member for Essex East also dealt with what we consider to be the contradictions and the confusions of Canadian policy in this field.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The confusion is all on the part of hon. members across the floor.

Knowing that hon. members opposite were not satisfied by our exposure of this confusion, perhaps I should document it in substantiation of what my friend the hon. member for Essex East said yesterday. I am now talking about nuclear testing. This is a matter on which we have a right to know the policy of our government without doubt, equivocation or uncertainty to the extent that security considerations make it possible.
On August 28, 1958 the Prime Minister made his first statement on this matter so far as I am able to ascertain. It was a statement made in the House of Commons. The hon. gentleman said:
The house will recall that on several occasions since I became Prime Minister I have advocated the suspension of nuclear tests, but always providing there was adequate international control to ensure the observance of the undertakings made in that connection.
Then on February 9, 1960 as reported at page 866 of Hansard the Secretary of State for External Affairs, repeating what he had said previously inside and outside the house -and I quote this as just one of a number of statements he made-said:
Our position is very clear, Mr. Speaker; we are against further nuclear tests, period.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is still the government's policy.

I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to reconcile those two statements when he replies. I believe that I and some other hon. members on March 21

of this year, as reported at page 2251 of Hansard, asked the Prime Minister to reconcile what we thought were contradictions between what he said in 1958 and what was being said in 1960. The Prime Minister replied:
I see no contradiction in the viewpoint expressed today and that expressed two years ago, except that naturally with the events that are now taking place modifications become necessary in order to meet changing conditions.
Will the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who said there has been no change, explain what that means? I should be fair to the Prime Minister and read the rest of his reply. The hon. gentleman went on to say:
Possibly what I have said should not be considered as a modification. What it is in fact is an interpretation of an actual reality existing today.
That was on March 21, 1960; yet the communique which was put on the record yesterday, issued in Washington by the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Canada, read in part as follows:
Particular attention was paid to the importance of achieving, with effective international control, an end to nuclear testing-
Notwithstanding the communique which had just been issued a few weeks before, on June 7, 1960 at page 4599 of Hansard the Prime Minister is reported as saying:
We have made it very clear that we believe in the complete termination of nuclear tests.
I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs, does he not think there is some confusion between these various statements?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is all in the hon. gentleman's mind.
Let me try the hon. gentleman on another aspect of this problem, that is the question of non-military tests, which is a matter of practical importance in Canada because of our tar sand interests.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the Leader of the Opposition whether his party is in favour of more nuclear tests?

Mr. Chairman, the minister will find an answer to his question in Hansard if he wants to read it. About a year or a year and a half ago I put our position on the record. I said that we thought the time had come when the west should have a moratorium on tests irrespective of what the Russians did. That is clear. I went on to say that at the end of that moratorium-I mentioned a period of two or three years-when no western power would have nuclear tests irrespective of what the Russians did, we should reexamine the situation. That is clear and unequivocal. I wish the minister would make a statement of policy equally clear and unequivocal.
Supply-External Affairs
Now to look at the question of non-military tests, a matter of practical importance; on March 17, 1960 the Prime Minister had this to say on the subject:
In so far as an explosion in the Athabaska tar sands is concerned, I think it is some two years ago that I spoke on this matter and pointed out that while it was desirable that there should be a suspension of tests, those tests whose purpose was the advancement of the general good should for civil purposes be expected.
Then on May 13 the minister is reported in the Ottawa Citizen as having had this to say:
External Affairs Minister Green, Thursday snuffed out any hope of an early experiment to recover oil from Alberta's tar sands by nuclear explosion. He said the government "has taken a firm stand against these explosions".
Perhaps the minister will clear up this apparent contradiction.
I apologize to the committee for detaining it so long, but I want to say a few words about the North Atlantic Treaty Organization with which the minister dealt in his opening statement.

Before the hon. member goes on will he allow a question? What is his view in regard to atomic tests for the purpose of determining the availability of resources, such as in the case of the Athabaska tar sands?

That is a perfectly fair and very important question. I would see no objection to nuclear tests for non-military, commercial or industrial purposes of that kind, provided that in every case those nuclear tests were announced, with all the details concerning them, to some international organization like the United Nations, and provided that anyone who wished to witness those tests was given an opportunity to do so. Perhaps official witnesses from the United Nations would be enough. If the tests were made in those circumstances and under those conditions I can see no reason for not holding them at all because, after all, are we to say that this power, this energy, those explosive powers, shall never be used for any purpose? That might be the implication of the stand that we will not allow nuclear tests for any purposes. There may be times when we shall be very glad to have nuclear testing for non-military purposes, for peaceful purposes.
When I talked about NATO-I think it was in February that we discussed external affairs -the minister criticized me, after following me, because I criticized, at least I tried to point out, what I considered to be the weaknesses and some of the dangers that confront NATO. I have the minister's words here which I thought were a little unkind in the circumstances because what I had been saying
6366	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs had been said a few weeks before by Paul-Henri Spaak and by a lot of other people who are just as devoted to the ideals of NATO and its strength and its unity as is the minister himself. As a matter of fact, the minister said yesterday that perhaps I had not been so bad last February in the light of events that had transpired.
The Minister of National Defence said the other day he felt there was "a new feeling of cohesiveness in NATO," and I am quoting him. I hope he is right because nothing can be more important than to establish that feeling of cohesiveness. But because we feel it should be so is no reason why we should not be conscious of the threats and tendencies which are working against that cohesiveness. The minister assured me, he indicated it yesterday that it is important to do more than we have done, and he has spoken strongly and wisely on this in the last two years. It is important to do more than we have to develop nonmilitary co-operation inside NATO as Europe is developing non-military co-operation outside of NATO. If we do not show care and imagination we may find that the European nations inside NATO are so far ahead of the trans-Atlantic nations that fissures will begin to show.
The minister mentioned that a study was being given to what he called a 10-year program, a 10-year plan. No doubt that is all very useful, and perhaps it is a good thing that we examine the objectives and purposes of international organizations periodically; but I would remind the minister that surely it is more important now, rather than to study new problems and to plan new objectives, to carry out the recommendations that have been made in this field. The minister knows-I am sure he has looked at the report-that there was a pretty careful examination made as a result of a year's investigation by a committee of three which approached every NATO government for evidence and every NATO leader, both orally and in writing, spent a great deal of time consulting with NATO leaders, leaders of NATO governments, on what could be done to make NATO operate more effectively in the non-military field. That report, which is quite a long document, with a lot of recommendations, was adopted unanimously by the NATO council.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps NATO is like the United Nations. That means nothing is to be done about it.

It is not quite the same because we are friends in NATO and we start out with the assumption we try to carry out the recommendations; and they have to be unanimous in NATO, as the minister


knows, otherwise you would not get any recommendations. Therefore, there are proposals which have been accepted by the governments to strengthen NATO in the nonmilitary field. It is more important, I suggest, to try to get the governments to implement those proposals which we have accepted than to worry about new committees and new examinations or even new NATO summit conferences.
I still feel as I have always felt that as a centre for exchanging information and coordinating attitudes the NATO council has been valuable and important, but we have not yet come even close-this is not a criticism of the government because we were, I forget how many years, dealing with NATO when we were in office, it would apply to both sides of the house-to realizing a NATO council of ministers that would or could take collective political decisions to be confirmed by their legislatures, create a collective policy which would at least be something less than the least common denominator of the individual policies of the member states. I said a few weeks ago in speaking about this outside the house:
There still remains, 1 believe, a chance to move into a new phase and make of this coalition a unique venture in relations among sovereign states. Indeed if this is not done, then NATO is not likely to survive. If it fails then we will fall back on defence policies based on old concepts of national sovereignty and national control. These will certainly prove inadequate to meet the tests ahead.
This brings up the question of NATO and the military strategy which was raised yesterday, and which would require examination; it brings up the question of disengagement which was raised yesterday by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I think we should examine very carefully and sympathetically proposals for disengagement as a possible solution of the difficulties and the easing of tensions in Europe. It brings up also the whole question of our whole position in NATO, if you like, NATO and Canadian neutralism.
We had a speech this morning devoted almost entirely to this idea of Canadian neutrality in the battle between the giants in the world. I do not believe it is desirable or possible for Canada to be neutral in the world today, between the free democratic western forces and the communist dictatorships. Neutralism to me at least implies that we put the two super powers, the United States and the U.S.S.R., the leaders of the coalitions, on the same level of political morality, of freedom and of Canadian interest. That is what neutralism must mean, as I see it, and that is what I cannot accept; but that does not mean that we

should not within the coalition do our best as an independent voice to make sure that the western coalition follows the right policy. Surely that is the best role for Canada to play, as she has been trying to play it ever since 1945. One could call neutralism disengagement from NATO, if you like, but I cannot think that that would be of any help to peace or any assistance to Canada in realizing its national destiny. There is no rescue, there is no relief from our problems, as I see it, in falling back on neutralism.
One cannot talk about neutralism, of course, without talking about our relations with the United States because I suspect-in fact, I know as other members know-that the United States and its policies and its power are the very reason why there are some people in Canada who want a policy of neutralism at the present time, although perhaps not as many as the publicity that they get would suggest. But the United States is also one reason why, even if we wanted neutralism, it would be to say the least very difficult for us to be neutral and have our neutrality respected. The United States has therefore a pull both ways.
I cannot myself see any salvation or any hope in that kind of foreign policy because of our relations with the United States, our European friends and two mother countries. But I do feel, and I have said this before in the house and out of the house as have other members of the house, that we have to be more careful as the months go by in examining and assessing our position inside the coalition and particularly our relationship with the United States of America and which has reflected itself in recent months by the difficulties-I assume they are difficulties-that we are having with regard to the working out of arrangements for continental defence.
I had hoped, as other members have, that in the communique on the defence conference which was held this week at the Seigniory club we might have had more indication of government policy in this vitally important matter. The defence leaders of both countries were there, and while I know they could not be asked or expected to tell us the details of defence discussions I had hoped that perhaps we could have had some of the principles on which these discussions were based, outlined and emphasized. I had also hoped that we could have been given some information with regard to the application of these principles to defence and particularly to the use, if we use them, of nuclear weapons.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What about security?

I have already said to the minister, within the limits of security. I am asking for no more than that on this or any 79951-0-402
Supply-External Affairs other occasion. Perhaps the minister will be able to answer some of these questions in this field of nuclear weapons and continental defence. We ask ourselves the question: Are we or are we not going to use them for such defence? Are they necessary or are they not? We have been told by the Minister of National Defence-I do not want to get into the details of defence policy because that will be done later-and we were told the other day by the United States secretary of defence in his press conference in Ottawa that to be effective the Bomarc missile, on which we are going to rely at least in part for our defence, must have a nuclear warhead. We do not know whether it is going to have a nuclear warhead in Canada. We do not even know whether or how, if it has a nuclear warhead, it is to be used.
We have been told by the Prime Minister that we are negotiating with the United States on the conditions which would govern the use of nuclear weapons by Canada if a decision should be reached by the government to use them. I think I am fair in that statement of the Prime Minister's position. We were told two years ago that these negotiations had begun. Are we negotiating now or are we not? If we are not negotiating, what is the purpose of these meetings which have been going on now for a couple of years and which the Minister of National Defence called negotiations at one time and discussions at another time?
If these negotiations or discussions or whatever you wish to call them are going on with the United States, and they obviously are, will the Secretary of State for External Affairs tell the committee when he replies why the external affairs department is not taking part in them except in so far as the negotiations are concerned with the storage of nuclear weapons at Goose Bay and Harmon field? I understand that those negotiations have got to a point where perhaps letters can soon be exchanged and therefore external affairs is actively pursuing them now. Does external affairs take part in negotiations only when all the principles have been agreed on and is external affairs, the civilian agency of foreign policy, called in only at that time? If not, why has external affairs not taken charge of these discussions and negotiations with regard to the use of nuclear weapons which, if they are to be used according to the terms which the Prime Minister has outlined in the house, must require changes in congressional legislation in Washington. Eventually this matter will then have to come before the state department and external affairs so I suggest it is very unwise for the Secretary of State for External Affairs not to take part in negotiations respecting this vital matter and to leave

Supply-External Affairs these negotiations or discussions, if you want to call them that, exclusively to the officers of the Department of National Defence.
Perhaps members of the committee will forgive me if I tell them a story. I once sat next to Mr. Khrushchev at a dinner in Russia and I made some reference to Mr. Molotov who was sitting across the table. He said, "Don't pay any attention to what Molotov says. He is only a diplomat. We only call him in when the treaties have to be written. They know the words." I have too great respect for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to suggest that he will ever allow himself to be put in any such position but I should also like to ask him to tell us now, in the light of the importance of these negotiations, what part he is playing in them and what decisions, if any, have been reached.
I should like to say something about the commonwealth. I have far exceeded my time but I must mention this because the minister might accuse me of being unfriendly to the commonwealth if I did not make some reference to it. I share his assessment, as I have before, of the value of the new commonwealth, and I was interested to note yesterday that he has begun to realize some of the difficulties that are inherent in the organization of the new commonwealth. I was glad to hear him emphasize, as other members have, the importance of the scholarship exchange. This is the kind of thing that pays dividends in the future. I also share his hope that we can have more and more of these scholars go to our French speaking universities so that when they go back to their countries they will realize that Canada is a country of two languages, two cultures and two traditions but one unity. I was glad to hear him say that everything was being done that could be done to that end and I know some of the difficulties in directing scholars to French speaking universities.
The minister asked for our advice yesterday about some of these commonwealth problems, and that was a refreshing and encouraging departure. Maybe the Minister of Labour will be doing that one of these days. He pointed out that before long we will perhaps have in the commonwealth Cyprus, which is about to apply for membership, Malta, the West Indies, Rhodesia, Uganda, Tanganyika, Kenya and, of course, Nigeria. He wondered whether the value of informal consultation around the table might be affected in some way, and this is a very legitimate preoccupation on his part, by the inclusion of a number of new members of the commonwealth, some of which will be small in population and will emphasize by


their appearance the disparity in size, population, interest and responsibilities between members.
If I were the minister I would not worry too much about that. After all, in the twenties when the population of New Zealand was only about a million and Great Britain was the great power in the world there was no difficulty in reconciling the interests, and the desire to be of assistance, of New Zealand and Great Britain. Perhaps the presence around the table of these new representatives of new nations, even though some are small, will emphasize the new value of the commonwealth as an association of friends of all sizes, all races and all creeds and as a bridge between the new nations and the old nations, the new world and the old world.
One thing I am convinced about, and the minister brought this up himself, is that it would be unwise and quite impractical to have two types of membership in the commonwealth or, as he put it, first-class and second-class citizens. I am not suggesting he recommended that but he said that was one possibility though I think he rather demurred at its practicability. The commonwealth will continue to be the valuable and important organization that it has been. It can get over difficulties of membership. If it does not have to choose between a member like South Africa and, if you like, Ghana, it may then have a great new field of usefulness. But if it runs into the rocks of racial discrimination then the commonwealth is going to have a very hard time staying afloat. Nobody would gain but the communists if it were not possible to keep it afloat; not only to keep it afloat but to keep it moving forward and to add new members to it.
I would also have liked to talk about the organization of American states, about which the minister did not say very much. Perhaps he will say something about it in reply. I wonder whether we can get the minister's views on this and whether they would conform to what he said outside this house some time ago, that we should join this organization.

I wonder whether the Leader of the Opposition would say, out of his experience, could the prime ministers' conference, in view of the variety of colours and races that will ultimately be characteristic of the commonwealth and the diverse attitudes that may exist in various parts of the commonwealth, discuss these matters privately if there were no communique required indicating unanimity? Would that be a sensible suggestion?
That is a very difficult question because it is such an important question.
On the basis of your experience?

On the basis of my experience-my experience covers a period when commonwealth relationships were simpler than those relationships are now. We did not have these particular problems facing us which result of the admission of new members from Africa, although in my day we did have the association of Pakistan and India.
Canada, as the Prime Minister knows, was one of the leaders in arranging the formula which made it possible for a republic to come into the commonwealth. In those days, it would have been impossible to conduct a prime ministers' conference on the basis of any formal, voted decisions, being reached, either on the basis of unanimity or a majority decision. I cannot see anything but danger ahead if decisions are taken by votes at commonwealth meetings. I would hope it would still be possible, in the days ahead, to continue the practice of informal discussions around a table trying to arrive at a concensus on the issues that are brought up. If that is not possible, then those in the majority merely try to bring pressure to bear by argument on the minority, and let it go at that. If the time comes when a member of the commonwealth violates the principles of free democratic association, internationally and nationally, on which the commonwealth is based, if any member of the commonwealth continues to do that it will of course be quite impossible for that member to remain a member of the commonwealth. Indeed, it would not be desirable that it should. I say that without reference to any particular situation at the present time.
We have, then, the situation where we have no formal voting, and therefore minimize in a purely formal sense the importance of the discussions in the interest of getting opinions around the table. We have to choose between that and the possibility of a more formal, more decisive type of voting meeting which might drive some members out of the commonwealth. I do not know whether that answers the Prime Minister's question, but that is the way I see it at the present time.
Mr. Chairman, I have gone on a long time. In fact, the length of my speech in the middle of July during the lunch hour has been unpardonable, but I hope I shall be pardoned just the same.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before the Leader of the Opposition sits down, may I ask a question? What would be his views concerning the use of 79951-0-402J
Supply-External Affairs nuclear warheads on Bomarcs under joint control of Canada and the United States?

Mr. Chairman, it is very difficult for me to answer that question because I would have to tell the minister whether I thought we should use Bomarcs at all. This is another question with which I expect to deal when we have our debate on national defence. If the decision of this government or any Canadian government is to use Bomarcs as a part of our defence and to equip them with nuclear warheads, I would hope-I have said this before-that the use of those nuclear warheads would be either under Canadian control or under coalition control. I would not find it easy to accept- I went further when I answered this question before and said that I could not accept a situation where a Canadian weapon, in the hands of a Canadian unit, a Canadian squadron if you like, could not be used without authority being given by the government of another country. This, of course, is what joint control means. It means that each side has a veto on the use of the weapon. In the case of the Canadian share of such control it would be the veto on the use of a Canadian weapon which we have in any event merely because of the fact it belongs to a Canadian squadron. In the case of the United States, it would be the veto of the use of a weapon of a Canadian squadron which would be something that I do not believe could be tolerated.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What does the Leader of the Opposition mean? I understood him to say he favours either Canadian control or, as he said, coalition control. He did not deal with the second.

I can deal with this verj simply. I have said before, and I will say again when the national defence estimates are being considered, that we have to bring North American continental defence under NATO control, and the position of Canadian units on this continent should be analogous to their position under NATO coalition control in Europe.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the debate on the administration item of this department has been one which would fit in with the words I used in my speech in February, "free-swinging". I think this is a very good thing. In earlier years very often the debates on foreign affairs policy have been insipid and not really Canadian at all. Now they are beginning to liven up and I hope the result will be that it will be much easier for the secretary of state for external affairs, whoever he may happen to be, to work out the details of Canadian foreign policy.
6370	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs
Does the minister recall the Suez debate?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I remember the Suez debate, and I am not backing water at all.
It was not insipid.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, but that was quite a long time ago. There have been very useful suggestions made by each one of the hon. members who participated in this debate. These suggestions will be given careful consideration by me and by the officials of the department. After all, conditions are such in the world today that Canada, like any other nation, cannot fail to consider every suggestion that is brought forward for meeting these tragic world conditions.
In my work as Secretary of State for External Affairs I am always trying to see that Canadian common sense is applied to the problems. It is quite easy, in this field, to get theoretical and to have ideas as to what might be done, thus getting one's feet far off the ground. I do not believe that Canadian foreign policy will ever get or retain the support of the Canadian people unless it stands up as being a very sensible kind of policy. I hope this will be the approach of all hon. members who have taken part in this debate, and that is quite a severe test.
There is another difficulty in that many of these problems involve security. It is not as though one could tell the whole story to the house and have it read by our allies and those who are against us without some harm being done. One very good example of that is the meetings of the ministerial committee on joint defence, one of which was held earlier this week. Almost everything that is discussed at those meetings involves the security of Canada and the United States, and perhaps in some cases of the whole free world.
The ministers participating are not in a position to make agreements or decisions; these have to come from the cabinets of the respective countries. I thought the former secretary" of state for external affairs had forgotten just what took place in this department, when he suggested that I should give a pretty full report of what took place at that meeting. This simply cannot be done.
Requests have been made for a statement about certain problems which are very critical at the present time, and one of these was the situation in Cuba. I agree with what different hon. members have said about the seriousness of this situation. There is no doubt that it could have very far-reaching effects on the whole of the western hemisphere and perhaps on even a wider field than that.

There is also no doubt that the Soviet union has a regular habit of trying to benefit from situations of this kind and has been working along these lines with regard to Cuba. Soviet leaders are pretending to be great friends of Cuba, and as hon. members know Premier Khrushchev even went so far as to say that if the United States did anything in Cuba missiles, presumably missiles with nuclear warheads, would be fired by Russia at the United States.
That is an extremely serious threat. One cannot imagine the President of the United States making a threat of that kind against any country in the world, but the United States has had that threat made against it within the last week or ten days. We all know our friends across the border and how they react. They are a proud people and this is not a threat that can easily be ignored either by the United States or any other country. Canadians would react pretty violently against the same kind of threat too.
So we have to try to understand the human reaction in these different countries. Canada's attitude with regard to the Cuban crisis has been to urge patience, discussion and negotiation and that heads be kept cool, having in mind the hope that in this way this very serious problem can be worked out without any further damage being done.
Our views have been made clear. The hon. member for Assiniboia wanted to know whether we had been making protests and all that sort of thing, but I would point out to him that discussions are going on between the United States and Canada daily on various problems. It is not a matter of our ambassador or members of his staff sitting in the embassy and then once a week writing a note about some matter and rushing to the state department to present it. There are the closest of contacts between the officials of the two governments and our views on the Cuban question have been made perfectly clear. When we met at Montebello this week this was one of the subjects which came up for review.
The Cuban question has been placed before the security council by Cuba, so there is to be a debate on it there. In addition there is the possibility that it will be taken before the foreign ministers meeting, I think it is, of the organization of American states. Whether it will be dealt with first in the security council or in the organization of American states we do not as yet know. I think there is some prospect that there could be successful deliberations under the organization of American states.
I think it was the hon. member for Assiniboia who spoke rather wildly accusing the United States of interfering because it was

protesting the action of Russia in trying to step into Cuban affairs. I point out to him that at the inter-American conference held at Bogota in 1954, a declaration was unanimously adopted by all of the members of the organization of American states which dealt with the question of communism in the western hemisphere. For example, the resolution carries the title "Declaration of solidarity for the preservation of the political integrity of the American states against the intervention of international communism". I will not read the whole resolution, but the first recital is as follows:
The American republics at the ninth international conference of American states declared that international communism, by its anti-democratic nature and its interventionist tendency, is incompatible with the concept of American freedom, and resolved to adopt within their respective territories the measures necessary to eradicate and prevent subversive activities.
One of the declarations contained in this resolution expresses the determination of the American states to take the necessary measures to protect their political independence against the intervention of international communism. Another declaration says that the domination and control of the political institutions of any American state by the international communist movement extending to that hemisphere the political system of an extra-continental power would constitute a threat to the sovereignty and political independence of the American states, endangering the peace of America and would call for meetings of consultation to consider the adoption of appropriate action in accordance with existing treaties.
So it is not just a case of the United States going much too far in its language and in its reactions. All the other countries which are members of the organization of American states are parties to this resolution, and this is a problem which they face in common.
I do not intend to deal with all the statements which were made by the hon. member for Assiniboia, but I am sure he was very unfair in his statements about the United States. I do not always agree with the stand taken by the United States, and perhaps Canada's greatest problem since the time of confederation has been to prevent the domination of Canada by the United States, but when we hear such violent accusations made against our neighbour as were made by the hon. member for Assiniboia this morning I can only say that I think they were in a large measure irresponsible and also unfair and unwarranted.
Another question I was asked had to do with events in the Congo. The Leader of the Opposition intimated that when I was making
Supply-External Affairs my opening remarks I should have dealt fully with the Congo situation. I point out to him that the house has had a blow by blow report by the government each day on the situation in the Congo as we knew it. Yesterday, on orders of the day, statements were made which set out the position as at that time, and I think it was a little rough of the Leader of the Opposition to accuse me today of failing in my duty because in my remarks yesterday afternoon I did not repeat what had been said to the house about the situation in the Congo.

I hope the minister does not think I accused him of failing to discharge his duty. I merely said that I thought in the light of what was going on in the Congo he might have something more to say about Africa. I did not criticize the minister very strongly about that, and I certainly did not suggest he was defaulting in his duty.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Here again, on this question there has not been complete fairness toward the United States. The United States was asked earlier this week in a written request by the government of the Congo, signed by several of the ministers, to send, I think it was, 2,500 troops to the Congo at once. They gave consideration to that request. They consulted with the United Nations and decided that they would not accede to the request. Then the president and the prime minister of the Congo, who had been in some other part of the country at the time, came back to the capital and apparently signed a request to Premier Khrushchev and repudiated the request which had been made to the United States. Today we get reports of the reaction of Premier Khrushchev.
In the meantime, the United Nations had acted promptly and I think effectively and in a very wise way by deciding that forces should be sent in from different African countries. The first troups to arrive in Leopoldville came this morning from Ghana, under the command of a British general, by the way. United Nations observers will be en route from Palestine by Sunday, including two Canadians. Three more Canadians- I have just had word while I have been sitting here-have volunteered and I believe they will probably be going with the other two.
But now, after this has been done by the United Nations, after the problem has been faced and the first active steps have been taken by the United Nations, the soviet steps into the picture presumably in an attempt to get any credit that may be given around the world, and Premier Khrushchev has said that the Soviet union is ready to

Supply-External Affairs act to halt aggression in the Congo if those states who are carrying on direct aggression against the Congo do not stop their criminal measures.

May I ask the
minister a question so that we may know what is the source of this information. What is he reading from?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This is from a press dispatch which, incidentally, was given to me by the Leader of the Opposition this morning, but I have since had my own dispatches in. The Soviet premier is reported as saying:
If those states which are carrying on direct aggression against the Congo do not stop their criminal measures, the Soviet union will not hesitate to take decisive measures to halt the aggression.
This is very similar to the threat which was made at the time of Suez. It should be understood for what it actually is. The real move to settle the situation has been taken by the United Nations. Canada has done and will do her full share in bringing about some solution to this very difficult problem.
The hon. member for Assiniboia and the Leader of the Opposition were very critical because I had not dealt with the case of the plane which was shot down by the Russians, I think on July 1. The hon. member for Assiniboia accused the Prime Minister of sheer irresponsibility because of what he described as a failure to give the house a report of what had happened in that incident.
We have now had an opportunity to check the situation. There is no doubt whatever in our minds that this plane was shot down a good many miles away from Russian territorial waters. Young Americans were killed. Two are now prisoners. They were on a flight which under international law was perfectly proper. Under these conditions it does not make very much sense that hon. members of the Canadian House of Commons should make fantastic charges against the United States as was done by the hon. member from Assiniboia.
When the U-2 flight took place we protested to the United States. That was a clear case of a plane flying over the territory of another country and we made our objection to such a course known at once. In the other case we did not protest. From what the Leader of the Opposition said he was of the opinion that perhaps we should have done so. In any event that certainly was the view of the hon. member for Assiniboia.
Mr. Chairman, at no time did I suggest that we should have protested to the United States with respect to this incident.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I accept the explanation made by the Leader of the Opposition. This is another example of the need for Canadian members of parliament to keep their heads about these very difficult problems.
Both the hon. member for Essex East and the Leader of the Opposition took up their old battle cry about there being a division between the Prime Minister and myself with regard to the attitude of the Canadian government on nuclear testing. I have never been able to understand why these leaders of the Liberal party have so persistently thrown their weight behind a policy of not objecting to nuclear tests until there is an international agreement. That is what it amounts to.

Perhaps the minister will let me say this. I pointed out once again this afternoon that our policy on this side is to support a position by which nuclear tests would be abolished for a period of time even without control and inspection and even if the Soviet union and the communist countries did not come into that. That is clear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh, yes, the Leader of the Opposition explained that today. His policy is that there should be a moratorium but he very carefully did not say for how long a time.
I said two or three years.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: At the end of that time they would take a look at it again. That is not very much comfort for the Canadian people who are against nuclear tests. At the same time the Leader of the Opposition says that the government's policy is indefinite. It certainly could not be much more indefinite than the policy just enunciated by the Leader of the Opposition. Our policy has been that we are against further nuclear tests, period. We have repeated that time and time again but it does not seem to sink into the heads of the two Liberal leaders.
It does not sink into the Prime Minister's head.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Essex East quoted the communique issued by President Eisenhower and the Canadian Prime Minister but the hon. gentleman very carefully refrained from quoting the cross-examination which took place in this house the next day. I would refer the hon. members to Hansard of June 7, 1960 at page 4599 where the Prime Minister was questioned about this situation and used these words:
Mr. Speaker, there has been no change or suggested change along the line that has been advanced by the hon. gentleman. Canada's policy is completely unchanged.

The Prime Minister was questioned further. The hon. member for Essex East is a very-persistent questioner. It is not as though the hon. gentleman asked one question and sat down. He usually asks one question and when a point of order is raised the hon. member turns his back, looks the other way and goes on asking more questions. In this instance the hon. gentleman continued asking questions and finally got the answer he did not want. The Leader of the Opposition was one of the questioners on that occasion, as well. It was a dual attack by these two Liberal leaders.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Punch and Judy.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The final answer given by the Prime Minister was in these words:
We have made it very clear that we believe In the complete termination of nuclear testing.
I will not try to explain that any further because if the two hon. gentlemen do not understand it now they never will.

Would the Secretary of State for External Affairs permit a question on this particular point because I think it is desirable to get it cleared up even in our minds. I would ask the minister-and this will certainly clear it up-if there were an international convention on nuclear testing prohibiting it without provision for inspection and control would the government accept it?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government would continue to be against nuclear testing. We think there is great value in building up world opinion against nuclear testing.
Quite.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is one of the reasons we have taken this strong stand. Here you have possibly thousands of Canadian children who will suffer because of the nuclear tests which have already taken place. Much of the fall-out from the tests which have been held is not yet down from the atmosphere. No one knows just how terribly serious the question of radiation and fall-out may be. The government decided that the wisest course to follow was to make it absolutely clear that we are against further nuclear tests. The United States knows that and we explained it to them again this week. There is no doubt about it.

Would the hon. member permit a question. I agree with what the minister said when he quoted the questions and answers addressed to the Prime Minister on the matter of the cessation of tests but would the minister explain the language of the communique which clearly
Supply-External Affairs establishes that the president and the Prime Minister said they would work toward a cessation of tests within a system of international controls.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The communique, as I remember, said that it was hoped there would be a system worked out-
No, no; they would work toward that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -a system for international control. We are in favour of that too. We believe there should be an international control worked out but whether or not there is, we say that we are against further nuclear tests.

That is not what
the communique says.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have told the hon. member what the policy of the government has been and is, and if he does not believe it he can read as many communiques as he likes but that will not alter the fact. The policy is still as I have stated it.

They are not our
communiques.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This brings me to another point. There have been suggestions made about what action Canada could take to focus world attention on the need-it is much worse than a need, it is a vital necessity-of bringing about a relaxation of tension. I have been very grateful for these suggestions. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres made one proposal last night. Incidentally, the hon. gentleman made a very helpful speech. The Leader of the Opposition made a similar suggestion today and perhaps one or two other hon. gentlemen have spoken along the same lines.
It just may be that the one way in which tension can really be relaxed in this world will be by action taken in the United Nations to focus world opinion on this problem. Whether that can best be done by a gathering of middle powers remains to be seen. Frankly I do not think it could be accomplished in the way suggested by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, by the method of inviting representatives of all the nations except the United States and the Soviet union to come to Canada and here work out some plan whether or not it was within the United Nations.
I do not believe that that idea can be worked out, but I am not putting aside any of the suggestions made leading toward this objective. We shall certainly give this subject most careful thought, and Canada will do

Supply-External Affairs what she can to reach that objective. As a matter of fact, for some weeks now we have been working in the department on this very subject of ways and means that Canada could take to give leadership in the attainment of this particular objective.
There has also been some criticism of our failure to give sufficient leadership in the 10-nation disarmament committee. I think most hon. members, even those in the two opposition parties, will feel that that criticism was hardly justified. Canada was one of a team of five western nations. Yesterday I asked the hon. member for Essex East whether he thought that each one of those five nations should have put in a plan and then presumably have kept on putting independent plans in to the 10-nation committee. That obviously would have been a silly thing to do, and it was not done by any nation. But he intimates that Canada just tagged along with the other four western nations and really did nothing at all; she did not take an independent stand.
There is one thing I am delighted to find out as a result of this debate, and that is that my good friends opposite are now converted to the policy I suggested many months ago, namely that the time had come for Canada to take an independent stand. They are now throwing it back at me and asking, why did you not take a more independent stand? Last year they were all for Canada being an honest broker, and they scoffed at the idea that it was now time for Canada to take an independent stand in world affairs. Paul has seen the light on the way to Damascus once again, after 2,000 years. He is right with me on this independent stand for Canada, and I hope we shall be able to keep him there. It is a little difficult to keep him on anything, but we shall try to keep him on our side on this as we pursue this independent course.
You had better start pursuing it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In the disarmament committee we made our proposals to the other western four when the representatives were working out a common western plan. Some of them were accepted; some of them were not. They might have been put in at different stages of the plan than we would have wished them to be, but a western plan was worked out and Canada took a part in that western plan, as one of the five nations. That same course was followed throughout as the plan was presented. When the committee was meeting and discussions were taking place we played our full part in those discussions and when the committee adjourned until the summit conference would be held I went to Istanbul


and there I made to the five western foreign ministers certain proposals, which I outlined to the house when I came back, as to what course should be followed. For example, this policy of trying to work out balanced concessions between the eastern members and the western members, suggesting that some meetings of the 10-nation group should be held off the record because as it was everything was being taken down and everyone was speaking for the record, which sometimes happens in the case of hon. members across the way in this house.
Never over here.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Never on the government side, either. I made other proposals at Istanbul at the meeting of the five western foreign ministers. Canada was working as a member of a team, and as an important member of a team, and I think everyone across the country, except perhaps the hon. member for Essex East, is giving us credit for having played our full part. Before the committee was scuttled by the eastern members General Burns had advanced the Canadian plan for balanced concessions. We believe that that was a very sensible stand, and we hope that eventually some such plan will be followed.
I have had printed his speech as an appendix to Hansard and, in addition, yesterday I had a summary of the Canadian government's instructions to General Burns in the way of a reply to the Russian proposals of June 2 likewise printed as an appendix. But when we are operating as a member of a team, as we were in this case, it is not very wise to be going off in a direction different from that taken by all of our associates. The Leader of the Opposition has explained how difficult it is to deal with the Soviet union. They are very quick to pick up any divergence and turn it against the western countries. I do not feel very guilty about our so-called failure to follow this independent policy in the disarmament committee.
The hon. member for Essex East asked me whether Canada was going to join the organization of American states. I think the Leader of the Opposition said something about that this afternoon. This would be a big step in Canadian foreign policy. The Leader of the Opposition quoted me as saying that Canada should join, but that dispatch was not entirely accurate because I think the words I used were "It might be that the time had come for Canada to join the organization of American states".
Then, the minister was misquoted because I used the quotation that I had from the press.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I may not have made myself clear to the press, but certainly this was the intention, to put it that it might be that the time had now come for Canada to join this western hemisphere organization. We are doing everything we can to promote our relations with the Latin American countries. For example, we have already sent the head of the new Latin American division to Cuba, and this has been done within the last few days, to assist our ambassador there and to strengthen our embassy.
I believe there is some value in letting the Canadian people do a little thinking about the question of whether they want their nation to join the organization of American states in order that we may see what the reaction of public opinion will be. As I said, this is quite a big step forward or backward, depending on the viewpoint of the person making the speech. I think it would be a step forward but it is of sufficient importance to warrant some time being given for consideration of the matter by the Canadian people. I have been very much gratified by the interest being taken in the question. Some excellent speeches on this very subject have been made during the course of this debate. Eventually Canada can decide just what policy will be followed.
The hon. member for Kootenay West made some suggestions which were certainly very far-reaching. I thought some of them were a bit off the ground but I give him full marks for at least taking the trouble to think about these problems and to make some concrete suggestions. He thought that Canada should adopt the policy of becoming a buffer between the United States and the U.S.S.R. I do not know what his idea of a buffer is but in my opinion it means that you get bumped pretty hard on each side and you do not have very much to say to the people who are doing the bumping. I doubt whether it would be a good thing for the Canadian government to adopt a buffer policy.
He also, of course, was very strongly opposed to NORAD. In the situations that we face I cannot agree with him about that. He wanted the D.E.W. line internationalized. He wanted us to invite the Russians to sit in on the D.E.W. line. If they would let us sit in on their D.E.W. line the suggestion might make some sense, but that was not his proposal. It was a one-way proposition. I suppose there would be Russians, Americans and Canadians at all the D.E.W. lines posts across northern Canada. That might create some very interesting conditions and bring about some rather interesting results but I am afraid that any such policy would have to be on a reciprocal basis and that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National
Supply-External Affairs Resources would have to send some of his officers to the D.E.W. line in northern Siberia. Of course, that was not the proposal.
He also suggested a zone in Europe, and I was somewhat surprised to hear the Leader of the Opposition support that proposal. It was described as a proposal for disengagement, and the hon. member for Kootenay West referred to the Rapacki plan. In urging a policy of disengagement by Europe the Leader of the Opposition at the same time emphasized the need for a closer tie with our allies in NATO. Surely he knows that West Germany and some of the other members of NATO take a very dim view of the Rapacki plan and they believe that the policy of disengagement is designed primarily to injure them. This certainly would not be a very good way to bring about good feeling in NATO.

I was not talking about the Rapacki plan and never even mentioned it. I referred to disengagement as something that should be considered by NATO and I had in mind the plan put forward in 1954 by Sir Anthony Eden involving a measure of disengagement which got a good deal of support at the time, but not the Rapacki plan in any way, shape or form.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition also made some comments about the plan of the three wise men for NATO.
I never called it that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He was very modest. He did not say that he was one of the three wise men.
It was a good plan.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He does not want anything like a 10-year plan now. He wants to go back several years and adopt the wise men's plan.
It is already adopted.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I understood him to say it should be adopted.
No, it was approved years ago but nothing was done about it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh, it was approved but he did not think anything had been done about it.
Very little.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He wanted Canada to take the position that rather than working on a 10-year plan that would cover the next 10 years the NATO nations should be going back several years and working on this somewhat outdated plan brought in by the three wise men. I give him full credit for the work that he and his associates did in preparing that plan but there are different conditions to

Supply-External Affairs face today. Some of the conditions were in existence at the time that plan was worked out but there are new conditions now. The world has changed a good deal in the intervening period and we believe it is essential that new methods should be devised and that the whole situation should be carefully reviewed in 1960.
As I said, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres made a very thoughtful speech and so did the hon. member for Megantic. We had him with us at the United Nations last fall as an observer. He made a splendid contribution and I thought his speech this morning was of a very high order. He complained that Canada had abstained too much in the voting at the United Nations, particularly in the fourth committee dealing with trusteeships. Of course, he is entitled to that opinion although I do not think he is quite right. We did play an extremely active and useful role in the fourth committee. The hon. member for Queens was the Canadian representative on that committee and has been for two years and is regarded at the United Nations as having done an extremely good job in that committee. The same is true, by the way, of the hon. member for Durham who for two years has been our representative on the second committee having to do with economic and trade matters.
We were co-sponsors of many resolutions dealing with the great development in the African progress toward full freedom and independence. For example, the Canadian delegation was especially in the forefront of negotiations which brought about an advance from October 1 to July 1 in the date for ending the trusteeship agreement respecting Somaliland. The Canadian delegation hailed the new state and expressed pleasure at sharing our national day with that country. Our initiative with respect to the commonwealth scholarship plan has been and is very much appreciated by the leaders of the African people and we think it will bring in a growing number of people from the African continent. However, I will be glad to take a second look at the actions taken by Canada in the fourth committee. We appreciate the criticisms, but I think the delegation has done very well, certainly in that particular field.

May I ask the minister a question at this point? If he recalls, I also criticized the Liberal government which abstained from voting in earlier committees, just as this government did. Can the minister say whether it had already been decided that these two nations of which he spoke were to be admitted, or if they were asking to be admitted?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I agree that the hon. member
was very fair throughout his whole speech. He did criticize both the present government and the government of his own party.
He is always fair.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I think that is true. He
mentioned again the need for contacts between Canada and the French speaking countries in Africa. He suggested that there could be technical people, teachers and various technical personnel, sent out to these countries. With these proposals generally I heartily agree. I do not know at the moment just what can be worked out, but we are concerned with the problem and will be doing what we can.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm also had some very useful suggestions dealing with western hemisphere problems. Then I come to the hon. member for Assiniboia. I think I have dealt with most of his statements. He was extremely emphatic today. I am afraid he is becoming more emphatic every week, and he is a good deal more effective when he is not so emphatic. At the very end of his speech he raved about Canada now being in the hip pocket of President Eisenhower. Canada is too big to go in President Eisenhower's hip pocket. This is not the situation at all; we are not in anybody's hip pocket at the moment, and we do not intend to be.
I said Canada's foreign policy was resting in President Eisenhower's golf bag.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is even worse than what I thought he said. I do not believe many people would take the hon. member too seriously when he makes that statement.
The hon. member for York Centre also had some very useful suggestions. He reminded us that Canada has a large reserve of young men in her universities, well trained and anxious to face the challenge of going abroad to help the underdeveloped countries of the world. I thought the hon. member brought forward a very worth-while idea. We shall be seeing what we can do to work out some plan along that line.
I believe that covers most of the points which were raised. The Leader of the Opposition did intimate that the secretary general or a representative of the United Nations should be present at meetings outside the United Nations, for example at summit meetings. I would remind him that as a result of Canada's initiative there was a representative

of the United Nations sitting in on the meetings of the 10-nation disarmament committee. We agree that the United Nations should be kept connected as closely as possible with all of these deliberations; that will be the policy followed by the government.
Finally, there were various questions asked about nuclear weapons and about the part that the Department of External Affairs plays in the discussions and negotiations on these questions. I do not doubt but that when the Leader of the Opposition was the secretary of state for external affairs there were discussions going on at the official level between Canada and the United States on the question of nuclear weapons. Now it is intimated that a different course is being followed from that which was followed under the former government. The statement that the former government had nothing whatever to do with nuclear weapons is, I suggest, merely pretence. They had that actual situation at that time and I believe the discussions between Canada and the United States concerning nuclear weapons started at the official level while the Liberal government was still in power.
The same thing is true of NORAD. Sometimes we are accused of initiating the NORAD agreement, but practically everything had been done before the former government went out of office. So there is quite a bit of hyprocrisy involved in the stand now being taken by hon. members opposite. As they know, we are in an alliance with the United States, and with many other nations, and discussions take place at the official level daily. This situation will continue as long as Canada is in these alliances. As I have explained before, and I repeat today, when it comes to the actual working out of the agreement in writing, that becomes the responsibility of the Department of External Affairs. We have a defence liaison division in the department. It is, of course, cooperating with the Department of National Defence. Really, there is no mystery about this whole situation as my hon. friends opposite would have the Canadian people believe.
I believe I have dealt with the various questions which have been brought up. I shall be glad to try to answer any other questions on the different items. Once again, may I say that I believe there is great value in a discussion of this kind in the Canadian House of Commons on foreign policy. I do not expect to be able to work out a foreign policy with which everybody in this house will agree; that just cannot be done. However, it is of tremendous assistance to be able to
Supply-External Affairs come to the floor of the house and have members get up and say what they think Canada should do. We shall use our best judgment with regard to the different proposals that have been made. I hope that in the days that lie ahead Canada will have no reason to be ashamed of the stand that is taken by those Canadians who happen to represent her at the time.

Item agreed to.
7B. Representation abroad-operational-including authority, notwithstanding the Civil Service Act, for the appointment and fixing of salaries of high commissioners, ambassadors, ministers plenipotentiary, consuls, secretaries and staff by the governor in council, $10,042,971.
Mr. Chairman, I see there is an increase of nearly $500,000 for representation abroad. Perhaps the minister would indicate what is responsible for that increase.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
One reason for the increase in this vote is the fact that we are providing for the first time this year for the new post in Nigeria. Our commissioner has been there for some time and we are setting up a full-fledged post there.
Another reason is the increase in salaries, allowances and travelling expenses. The increase in salaries is $173,000. There is an increase in allowances of $90,000 approximately and in travelling expenses of about $30,000. In addition, telephones, telegrams and other communications services have gone up about $49,000. The rentals of land, buildings and works have increased about $173,000.

The minister talked last night about the desirability of completing our representation in South America and perhaps having a Central American embassy. Provision is not being made for that in these appropriations, I take it?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
Is there any likelihood of any mission being established in Baghdad or Ankara?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is a mission I would like very much to have established, and there are others too I would like to have established; but in getting these wishes carried out I always run foul of the treasury board. I do not doubt the Leader of the Opposition had that same problem when he was minister. I would like to have a mission in Baghdad right now, but so far I have not been able to make much progress.

Item agreed to.
6378	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs
77.
