Representation abroad-construction, acquisition or improvement of buildings, works, land, equipment and furnishings, and to the extent that blocked funds are available for these expenditures, to provide for payment from these foreign currencies owned by Canada and provided only for governmental or other limited purposes, $1,037,000.

I asked the minister on the last item to explain the increase, but on this item would he explain the decrease? I am not objecting to it, of course, but does this mean we are slowing down our embassy building program abroad?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We have been postponing some of our construction work abroad because of the budgetary position.

I appreciate the minister's difficulties with treasury board. I would have thought that perhaps he would be more skilful than I ever was in overcoming them, but I am sure the minister does not need anyone to tell him that while funds for capital construction abroad do add to the budget and the budgetary difficulties of the Minister of Finance, over the long run they are economical because the rentals of rented premises and all that kind of thing, while they may not be as much in any one year as the amount which would be required for an embassy, over a period of five or ten years require much more money than would be spent over that period if you had bought or built an embassy.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is exactly the argument I have been making with the Minister of Finance. Now that I have some support from the Leader of the Opposition perhaps it will be easier to convince him.
Perhaps I had better keep quiet.

Item agreed to.
78.	Canada's civilian participation as a member of the international commissions for supervision and control in Indo-China including authority, notwithstanding the Civil Service Act, for the appointment and fixing of salaries of commissioners, secretaries and staff by the governor in council, $255,958.

May I ask the
minister a question about this particular item. We have members on the civilian side of the international commission for supervision and control in the old Indo-China, Cambodia, Loas and in South Vietnam. What are the prospects of dissolution of these organizations in these three countries? What is the situation with regard to the adjournment sine die situation in Laos? What is the situation in Cambodia where there seemingly cannot be too much to do? The situation in South Vietnam of course is a little more


complicated and possibly there is no doubt about the desirability of continuing the commission there.
I can understand the difficulty about the use of forces from Canada and countries like Canada in the situation which now prevails in the Congo, but there are experienced military personnel certainly in South Vietnam and I presume in Laos; I doubt very much if there are any in Cambodia. But to the extent they are available, is any consideration being given to that, assuming their acceptability?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The commission in Laos, as the hon. member knows, was deactivated a long time ago and we have no one there at all.
No military personnel there at all?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. The Laotian government is still opposed to having the committee reconvene.
The commission in Cambodia is very small, but the commission in South Vietnam remains as it was and is very active. There is quite a lot of subversion in South Vietnam and unfortunately there is quite a bit of boundary problem between Cambodia and South Vietnam, and some question as to whether the commission is authorized to deal with problems of that kind. As I understand it, it has been called in to help with these problems. Canada does not think that it should be, but we are only one of the three nations represented on it.

Item agreed to.
Contributions to international economics and special
aid programs-
Bilateral economic aid programs-
86. Colombo plan, $50,000,000.

On this item, I wonder if the minister could inform the committee how much has been provided to Colombo plan countries. Can the minister give us a breakdown of how much has been provided in the past year? It would be helpful, also, if he could inform the committee with regard to any intention of the government to make further provision of this kind.
I should like to take one moment, if I may, to repeat what I said earlier today, namely that in 1957-58 a loan was provided to the Colombo plan countries of $35 million. This was used for the purchase of wheat and I think the transaction was mutually helpful both to Canada and to the Colombo plan countries. I am exceedingly disappointed that we should have allowed the United States to take the lead in this field almost to the complete exclusion of Canada. I think the policy

which has allowed this to happen has been a very shortsighted one. We would like some illustration of the government's views with regard to any other plans which it may be considering by way of economic aid, particularly the provision of food, for the Colombo plan countries.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am getting the figures with respect to the wheat that was given under the Colombo plan. Loans for the purchase of wheat would be a question for the Department of Trade and Commerce. They primarily involve that department.
Or the Department of Finance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It may be the Department of Finance, I do not know; but they do not come under the Colombo plan at all.

A great deal of what was
covered in the committee has been dealt with again this afternoon, and that may be all to the good. The question of the Colombo plan was among those which were raised and after a somewhat unenthusiastic approach by the persons involved a report was forthcoming which satisfied me and one or two other members of the committee who were interested.
I should like to ask the minister what progress has been made with the visual chart requested showing the comparative contributions of Canada, on a per capita basis, as compared with those of other western nations and members of the communist bloc. I appreciate the magnitude of such a project, but I wonder if the minister could perhaps give us a progress report.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The information which is available to the department on this question was given in the committee. We are working on the suggestion put forward by the hon. member, but apparently nothing is ready yet.
It might be helpful if I reminded hon. members that the western nations are very far ahead of the eastern nations in their aid at this time. The Soviet union has been following a policy of making loans, but when it comes to gifts of the kind covered by the Colombo plan the western nations have a very much better record than the eastern countries, and I do not think any country has a finer record than has Canada. We are spending $50 million a year on the Colombo plan.

The reason I raised the question in the committee is that a great number of my constituents are aware of various generalities about this subject and what I, as well as one or two other members wanted, was a visual chart so that Canada's position could be stated visually. I certainly propose to use this at meetings in my constituency and other
Supply-External Affairs places to demonstrate more effectively and dramatically just what Canada is doing.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is a very useful suggestion and I think we can work out something of that kind.

I saw figures of that kind in graphic form a little while ago, I think it was in a report of one of the American foundations-the Rand Corporation or something like that. These figures make it clear, as the minister has just said, that though the Russians do a lot of talking about aid, the amount of aid they have actually given as compared with the western countries is small. Of course, the Russians have made skilful propaganda use of whatever they have contributed. For example, they pave the main street of a town, and the natives, instead of walking in the mud, walk on smooth pavement that the Russians have given them, and they all know about it. The western nations are more likely tc build a power station 25 miles away, in the hinterland, and despite its usefulness not very much is known about it.
This figure of $50 million cannot include the kind of assistance by way of loans made in order to buy wheat to which the hon. member for Assiniboia referred. Such loans would not come under the terms of the Colombo plan, though perhaps it could be done in some other way. It would be interesting to know how much of this $50 million represents capital and technical assistance, which was what the Colombo plan was set up to provide, and how much represents assistance in the form of consumer goods for which counterpart funds have to be established and, in the latter category, what was the form of the consumer goods provided-wheat, flour, and so on. I think that information would be useful.

The minister has said quite correctly that loans would not come under item 86, but I should like to point out that his department does take credit for what the government has done in this regard. I refer in particular to the tables which appear in the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the external affairs committee for Friday, March 11, where under a heading "Canada's financial assistance budget, 194161" are listed not only the Colombo plan and other programs involving goods but all the loans that the government has made over that period. So while such loans may not technically come under the minister's department they are, nevertheless, so closely allied with the other provisions that

Supply-External Affairs are made that they are included in the information which was supplied by the department.
It has been said by the minister, and by the Leader of the Opposition, too, that the assistance we have been giving in the field of economic aid has been much greater than that provided by the U.S.S.R. I am glad to have that assurance and I hope it is in every way factual.
I recall hearing on the radio not long ago that the U.S.S.R. made a long term loan to India. If my memory serves me correctly it was in the amount of $375 million at an interest rate of 1\ iper cent. Our $50 million gift is certainly not a loan. Perhaps these things cannot be precisely compared. From time to time we have been informed that some of these countries prefer to receive assistance by way of low interest loans rather than by way of gifts because they then feel under no particular obligation to the lending or donor country.
Can the minister give the committee any information as to the amount of loans currently being made by the U.S.S.R. to Colombo plan countries, shall we say? Canada should do more in this field. This group takes the stand that 1 per cent of our gross national product allocated for economic assistance in all forms would not be too much to ask of the Canadian people. This might work out to an amount of some $300 million annually. In relation to a $50 million Colombo plan gift or the total in the estimates under the general heading "Contributions to international economic and special aid programs" in the amount of some $61 million it represents a tremendous increase. Nevertheless it is not too large compared to the amount we spend for national defence. One per cent would still be a relatively small amount. The government should increase this kind of assistance. This group considers this money well spent both from the standpoint of advantage to Canada and the standpoint of the countries in receipt of the moneys. Greater emphasis in this field and less emphasis in the field of military expenditures makes good sense in 1960 as the best method of contributing to world peace.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I now have the figures for wheat under the Colombo plan. Last year 1959-60 it was $12.5 million out of the $50 million.
Do you have that figure in bushels of wheat?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am afraid I am not that much of a farmer. I do not know how many bushels that covers. We have no agricultural experts in our department.

The Leader of the Opposition asked for details of the way in which the money was spent, how much for wheat and how much for technical assistance and so on. I have here an example, the $25 million for India under the 1959-60 Colombo plan. That was allocated in this way: $11.5 million for metals; $7 million for wheat; $2.55 million for fertilizers; $120,000 for asbestos; $2 million for diesel engines for use in India; $700,000 for the Canada-India reactor; $130,000 for three more cobalt beam therapy units; $250,000 for telecommunications equipment. That was to help India build and bring its meteorological service into the world-wide weather reporting network. In addition $750,000 was set aside to carry out economic engineering studies on new projects which India had requested Canada to consider for future Colombo plan capital development programs and to finance the initial cost should any of the projects prove acceptable to the two governments. The division would not necessarily be the same in every year. It varies with the wishes of the recipient government and also with what is approved by the Canadian government.

Mr. Chairman, I am grateful for that information. Perhaps it was in the report of the committee and I should have recalled it. This may give me an opportunity to say for the record that one reason we are going through these estimates so quickly, involving as they do large expenditures, is that they were given thorough and careful examination before a committee.
I know that under the Colombo plan arrangements the details of contributions are worked out between the contributing government and the receiving government in each case. That is one of the important values of the Colombo plan type of aid. There is no question of imposing it or even of giving aid which seems to be in the form of an imposition and a charity.
I also know that in the negotiations that take place each year the contributing government can exercise a great deal of weight in what should be done. I want to ask the minister this question. Now that we are contributing more aid in terms of consumer goods in relation to capital goods and technical assistance is the minister satisfied that the receiving governments have not expressed any anxiety that this balance may not be shifting too far? In other words, are they satisfied not only with the amount-no, not the amount because no one is ever satisfied with the amount-but with the nature of the arrangement?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that is my understanding. The details are worked out with each different country. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, there is an agreement between the representatives of the country and the Canadian representatives. We try very hard to make the officials of the other countries perfectly happy about the plan.

Mr. Chairman, following the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia about the lack of effort on the part of the government to increase foreign assistance and decrease armament activity, apparently the C.C.F. group has not been paying close attention to the actions of this government. I notice by the estimates book, a copy of which I observe the hon. member has in his hand, that the estimates of the Department of National Defence are down $86,921,000 and the expenditures for foreign assistance are increased by $2,481,000 which seems to be consistent with the desire expressed by the hon. member.

I thank the hon. member for his interest in the policy of this group. The figures he used scarcely have any relevancy to what we have in mind. The government has reduced the defence estimates by $86 million-odd as has been pointed out and with this we have no quarrel but it has taken only $2 million-odd and added it to economic assistance while the balance has been used to bail out the Minister of Finance in his effort to balance the budget. That is not the kind of reduction we had in mind.
You reduce everything to the gutter.

The reduction of $86 million-odd has resulted in an increase in economic assistance of only $2 million. That is not the kind of thing I have in mind. I want to see a large reduction in the estimates for national defence and a large increase in economic assistance.
1 believe the minister said a moment ago that $12,500,000 had been provided this year for the purchase of wheat under the Colombo plan. I would say that would cover between 7 and 7J million bushels of wheat. The reason I am trying to convert dollars into bushels is that I have on my desk the figures in bushels for the previous years. Under both types of programs, so that there will be no argument, in 1957-58 Canada contributed to India, or provided India with 31.1 million bushels of wheat; in 1958-59 it was down to 18.2 million bushels of wheat; and this year it is only 7 million bushels.
I want to register the strongest possible objection to the trend that has set in under this type of program. I do not want to appear
Supply-External Affairs to be in conflict with the statement of the Leader of the Opposition that the Colombo plan essentially is for technical and capital assistance and that the provision of wheat and other food is brought about only at the request of the countries which are in receipt of the Colombo plan funds. Whether it be within or without the plan, I think more should be done in the field of providing wheat to Colombo plan countries. I think it is an atrocious situation that we are providing to India, a country of the commonwealth, this year under this program just over 7 million bushels of wheat, when the United States has signed a four-year loan program that will move into the Indian market 146 million bushels of United States wheat annually.
Judging from those figures, one would think that Canada had no surplus of wheat; that we had swept the granaries clean; that our elevators were empty; that our terminals were bare and that the whole problem had been solved. But what we are doing is permitting a reduction in the provision of wheat to India while the United States moves into this commonwealth market on a non-commercial or a semi-commercial basis, replacing Canada and taking over this very valuable market.
The minister of course will realize that if the trend of those figures continues, for all practical purposes next year we shall be excluded or we shall have excluded ourselves from the Indian market.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is an argument which really should be carried on by the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am told that India has never been a commercial market for Canadian wheat. I would point out to the hon. member for Assiniboia that half of the funds allotted to India under the Colombo plan went for wheat.
Not this year.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In 1959-60, $12.5 million. No, that was for all countries, but a very large proportion of the money provided for India was for wheat. I am responsible for the Colombo plan only; I am not responsible for getting rid of the prairie wheat. If we said to the Indian authorities, you must take so much wheat then, of course, we would destroy the whole good will value of the Colombo plan, and the hon. member is putting himself into that position.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We are discussing now the Colombo plan. It is essential to the success of the Colombo plan that the recipient nation should feel it is not having things forced on it. Whether there should be loans outside the

Supply-External Affairs Colombo plan is a different matter. I am not in a position to argue about that, but I do know that the other ministers whom I have mentioned have spared no effort to find ways of disposing of Canadian wheat.

What the minister has said is correct; he is responsible under this item for the administration of the Colombo plan only. However, the general heading is "Contributions to international, economic and special aid programs". The figures that have been provided by the department in this field range right across the board to include all forms of financial assistance. I am merely putting forth the argument on this item because it is certainly a related item. I realize quite well that a financial loan probably would not be under the Department of Trade and Commerce and certainly not under the Department of Agriculture; it would be under the Minister of Finance. Because of the customary way in which we discuss our estimates I am very much in order in saying on this item that it has been used and is being used for the provision of certain quantities of wheat, and that in my opinion the total over-all Canadian program is completely inadequate; it demonstrates that Canada has missed a great opportunity to assist a nation within the commonwealth on the one hand and to help reduce our surplus on the other. It demonstrates clearly that the opportunity was there. I point out that the United States has seized the opportunity. She is in the Indian market for wheat to the extent of 146 million bushels annually, guaranteed for the next four years.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question? Does he not feel that Canada, a nation of 17J million people, has played her full part in the Colombo plan and in the shipment of wheat to India?

No, Mr. Chairman, I feel that Canada has not played her full part. The best evidence of that is the mountain of grain from here to the Pacific ocean. If I may answer the question a little more fully, I said on another occasion I felt that Canada should have exerted every effort to obtain 50 per cent of the Indian market for wheat. In other words, of the 146 million bushels annually, Canada should be providing at least 73 million bushels. Therefore, I certainly disagree with the purport of the question of my hon. friend. I feel that what we are doing is exceedingly laudable. It has the support of all hon. members, but it is inadequate in the context of what we should do if the government would provide the required funds.

Is the minister in a position to report on the building of the atomic reactor in India? A lot of information has been bandied about, much of which has not been very complimentary to our efforts. I hope the minister is in a position to clear the air in this regard.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have the answer to that. With regard to the Canadian Colombo plan program in India, the committee will be interested to know that the Canada-India reactor, which Canada and India are building at Trombay, in India, went into operation last Sunday, July 10. The construction of the reactor, which is similar to the NRX reactor at Chalk River, was started in 1956, and Canada has made available approximately $9 million to cover the cost of the equipment and the training of Indian personnel. The successful completion of this project is a remarkable achievement and a great tribute to the engineers, scientists and technicians of Canada and India who have worked together in close co-operation for the past five years.
The reactor, which is expected to be fully operational this fall, is intended to provide scientists from India and other Colombo plan countries in south and southeast Asia with facilities for carrying out advanced research, for producing radioactive isotopes for use in medicine, agriculture and industry and for the training of students and technicians from India and other countries in southeast Asia. It is a matter of great satisfaction to the people of Canada and, I am sure, to the people of India that this unique project, which is devoted to the peaceful uses of atomic energy, has been carried forward to successful completion.

Is the minister in a position to tell the house what the original estimate of the cost of the project was and how much the cost actually turned out to be? I should also like to know who did the actual building. Were Canadian engineering firms involved and, if so, which firms?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I will have to get that information from the officials.

I should like to ask about another matter with which the minister is probably familiar. At any time has a serious complaint been lodged with the government with regard to the building of this reactor and, if so, would the minister indicate the nature of the complaint?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This question really should be asked when the estimates of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited are under consideration because the work was done under

their supervision. I am told that some disgruntled Canadian engineer has been writing letters and making complaints about the project but my department does not have the details.

Item agreed to.
87. West Indies assistance program, $4,510,000.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand that this vote includes the provision of two ships for the British West Indies. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that the construction of these ships appears to have bogged down completely. I should like to put on the record the statements of his predecessor and some of his present colleagues in the government. On June 17, 1958, more than two years ago, a question I had asked was answered by the minister's predecessor, Hon. Sidney Smith. His reply, which can be found at page 1281 of Hansard, reads in part as follows:
The detailed plans and specifications to which the question is directed have yet to be drawn up... The preliminary advice received is that the vessel will cost almost $2| million.
In August of the same year the Minister of Transport, as found at page 4270 of Hansard, made this statement:
We are preparing plans also for the construction of new ships for the Newfoundland coastal service operated by the Canadian National Railways and a new ship to be made available as a gift from the Canadian government to the new British West Indies Federation.
Then-this is very material-on September 23, 1958, according to Hansard of February 3, 1959, page 623, the Prime Minister issued a press release in which he announced that the Canadian government proposed to recommend to parliament that $10 million be made available to the West Indies over the next five years from Canada and that a sister ship would be built under this program as a partner to the first Canadian ship which Canada had already agreed to provide for the West Indians interisland shipping service.
It was clear in 1959 that two ships were to be provided. On April 16, 1959, as found at page 2740 of Hansard, the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave this information in answer to a question which I had asked him:
The designs of two passenger cargo type vessels have been prepared by a firm of ships' architects according to plans drawn up by officials of the West Indies government and accepted by officers of the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Transport. The designs have been submitted to a shipping expert named by the West Indies government. He has approved the designs, and specifications are now being prepared by the company of ships' architects and will be ready by May 15.
Supply-External Affairs
That was in 1959. He went on to say:
The ships will be built in Canadian shipyards, and it is hoped that they will be ready early in 1961.
As the minister knows, his colleague, the Minister of Finance, went to the West Indies and at Kingston, Jamaica, he made this statement on February 25 of this year:
The first major capital project which we undertook in our aid program consists of the gift of two ships to be used for interisland trading. The ships will cost over $6 million.
Then he gives a description of the ships, which I omit.
The design of the ships is complete. The laying of the keels should take place shortly.
These statements are in large part contradictory. In the first place, in spite of the estimate of the cost made by the predecessor of the Secretary of State for External Affairs the figure is now over $6 million or more than $3 million each, whereas the original cost for one ship was set at almost $2J million. According to the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the ships were to be ready early in 1961. The Minister of Finance now states that the laying of the keels should take place shortly and it is expected that the ships will be ready by the middle of next year. If the laying of the keels takes place shortly, the ships certainly cannot be ready in that length of time.
It is now two years since this statement was first made in the house concerning these ships. There is certainly something wrong with the plans and specifications and there is unquestionably a delay in connection with the matter. Could the minister tell the house what is delaying the construction of these ships, the reason for the different statements by several of his colleagues which are in part contradictory and why in effect it would not have been just as well to consider taking the six ships of Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships and transferring them to the West Indies? They would then have had them in operation at least two years ago.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Laurier had a very sad look on his face as he made these comments. I was wondering whether he was thinking about the William Carson which his government built for the Newfoundland service, which would not even go into the dock when it was built, and all the troubles they had in that regard. He should know better than anyone else in the house that sometimes there is a lot of trouble in connection with the building of ships. In the case of the ships for the West Indies there was difficulty in getting steel for the keels because of the United States steel

Supply-External Affairs strike. My information is that both ships are now scheduled for completion by the end of this year and that they will be in service next year.
I cannot guarantee that. I do not want the hon. member to quote these words against me a year from now because, as I have said, he knows it is sometimes very difficult to be accurate in one's forecast concerning the building of ships. As for the type of ship, I am not qualified to say whether or not the right type is being built. As I understand it, there was agreement between the Canadian authorities and the West Indian authorities and also I believe that the ships formerly owned by Canadian National Steamships would not be suitable for this particular purpose. In any event, I think they had been sold elsewhere.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to say a word in answer to the minister. I am aware of the difficulties which we had with the William Carson. I am also quite aware of the needling that came from this side of the house in connection with the William Carson which was an excellent ship and which has turned out to be-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: These might be good ships, too.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -one which is rendering yeoman service.
Has it ever sailed?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, the William Carson has sailed and is now in operation. I could call to my assistance any of the hon. members from Newfoundland who know it has turned out to be an excellent Ship.
However, the point I am making now is, first of all, here are five different statements made by the minister's colleagues, each one different from the other.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There were more statements than that about the William Carson.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, there was only one statement made, and it was made by the minister who was in charge of the department or by his successor. The Secretary of State for External Affairs now says the ships of Canadian National Steamships were not suitable. This is just not the case. They were suitable because that is where they operated. The Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships operated between the maritime provinces and the West Indies for 25 years, so those ships would have been suitable for that purpose. This would not have stopped the government to the slightest degree from putting the Canadian National ships into operation until the new ships were complete, if that course was more satisfactory to the British West Indies.

I might add, too, that the ships of Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, notwithstanding what the minister had said about them being sold, are down in Halifax lying idle. They are standing still, struck by-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the responsibility of the new owner.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is probably as a result of the policy of the Canadian government that they have not been able to deal with the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships in the manner in which they should. I did not mean to go into that because it is not a matter of concern to the Department of External Affairs. The only reason I have is that the minister used it in his reply. I think if the minister will press his colleagues he will find there is difficulty over designs with the West Indies federation, either transport or trade and commerce, in connection with the approval of the plans. Until that has been settled, I think it will take far longer than the minister anticipates. If this assistance is to be granted, it should be granted now and not in five years time.

It is always interesting to secure evidence indicating how experience with official responsibility leads to an understanding and a comprehension on the part of the minister, even of the William Carson.
I wanted to say a word about this vote because it represents a considerable increase, and an increase which we on this side support. We support it because it indicates a recognition of our increased interest in what is going on in the West Indies federation and it represents an attempt on the part of the government which, I think, is a serious one, to show our appreciation of the importance of this development, and to do what we can to assist it.
I am not at all sure, Mr. Chairman-it is not easy to establish priorities and you cannot do everything in government you want to do -if it would not be wise on our part to keep developing our aid and assistance to the West Indies federation even if it might mean, because of the limitation of our resources for this purpose, a cutting down perhaps in some respects in the future our aid to some other parts of the world. The West Indies are close to us. There is a historic and traditional connection between Canada, especially the Atlantic provinces, and the West Indies. I think we should maintain and develop this connection.
The proposal that we join the organization of American states has a bearing on this.
I do not know what the Federation of the West Indies, when it comes into existence

and is completely responsible for its own external relations, will do. I do not know whether it will join the organization of American states. If and when Canada does join this organization, and I do not quarrel with the minister's decision that this is something to which careful consideration should be given-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I ask the Leader of the Opposition whether he thinks we should join this organization?

I was hoping for guidance from the minister, especially in view of the statements he has been making and the trips he has been taking. He has decided, in his wisdom, that public opinion should be allowed to brood over it a little longer. Public opinion has had a long time to brood over the joining of the American states. I am not criticizing that. One result of joining the organization of American states would be that we would be considered by those states as a kind of rich North American contributing partner, and we would certainly have to be that. We would want to participate in any form of economic assistance that might be agreed upon by the organization. The United States is doing a great deal of that at the present time.
It is for this reason I mention what I consider to be the desirability of increasing our assistance of every kind to this new nation which will be within the commonwealth. I think anything the government can do in that regard, and this government shows that they are doing more than they were doing last year at least, certainly will receive the support of this side.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We are still in the process of working out the gift of $10 million. As the Leader of the Opposition knows, there is a close tie between these islands and Canada dating back a great many years. I do not think there is any doubt but that every consideration will be given to providing whatever assistance is possible.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a comment in connection with this vote. Normally, I would do it in the French language. In view of what the minister has said, there are just one or two brief remarks I should like to make. I, of course, agree
Supply-External Affairs fully with the item under discussion and commend the government for the idea of establishing these commonwealth scholarships. But I must find myself, in part, in disagreement with what the minister said in the course of his statement. What I shall have to say I hope he will find constructive.
I begin, first, by recalling to him that a vigorous protest was made by one of the directors, I think his title is director of scholarships, in the Canada council of arts and sciences, Mr. Toupin, about which I asked a question in the house while the minister was absent and which was handled by the Minister of Finance. At that time the director, Mr. Paul Toupin, took very serious objection to this program as regards Quebec. He had just attended a conference of the delegates of the association of Canadian universities which took place in Ottawa in connection with these scholarships. This statement was a very categorical one. He went so far as to say that the province of Quebec was not properly treated and that he declared, in his capacity as a director of the division of scholarships of the Canada council, that the universities of Montreal and Laval would not receive very much from the 200 scholarships which the Canadian government would grant and spend approximately $1 million thereon.
It now turns out that he was not so far off base. The Minister of Finance in answer to the question I put following the statement made by Mr. Toupin which appeared in La Presse of Montreal on May 4 denied the allegation. The minister has stated that there will be this year 104 scholarships granted. Four students will be going to Laval University and three to Ottawa University. That means four out of a total of 104, which is certainly not a very substantial proportion for the province of Quebec.
Here is where I find myself in disagreement with the minister, and it may well be that I have misunderstood his words or that they do not bring about the meaning which I put upon them. At page 6295 of yesterday's Hansard, when dealing with this question the minister is reported as having said:
There are not a great number of French speaking students across the commonwealth and some way will have to be found to meet the situation.
I disagree with that approach. It may be strictly true that there are not very many French speaking students who come from the commonwealth, but surely that is not the point. The point is that these students are coming here at the request of the Canadian government to advance their culture.
I can remember one day attending a state dinner and my neighbour was a delegate

Supply-External Affairs from India and to my great surprise he spoke to me in perfect French. I asked him how it was he knew French so well, and do you kow what he told me? He said "I have been following at Laval University in Quebec a course in French Canadian history". I said "Why do that when you live in India?", and he said "I am interested in the history not only of French Canada but of all countries, and I would like to be a specialist in that field".
So does it not boil down to this? I understand that it is not a matter for the government exclusively but is a matter within the committee I mentioned earlier. The committee can direct or assist or aid those students who do want to take post-graduate courses not to go to one university in preference to another but to point out to them that here, for instance, at Laval University are certain facilities, here at the University of Montreal are other facilities in which a student from a particular commonwealth country might well be interested, and here again at Ottawa university are still additional facilities.
While I speak of Ottawa university I think I can make this point in favour of it. It is the only university in this country I believe, unless I am mistaken, that has both the common law and the civil law courses. It is the only university which gives a degree in both common and civil law. That must of necessity have an attraction apart from all its other attributes.
But surely the University of Montreal with all the facilities it has and with all the modern faculties it has at its disposal should be given greater consideration, because of the seven students which the minister has mentioned, four will be going to Laval, three to Ottawa, but none to the University of Montreal. I do not say that in any destructive manner and I am sure the minister will not take it in that way, because he immediately added something which was extremely helpful. As reported on the same page of Hansard he said:
I am not yet In a position to say just how it will be done.
Meaning assistance.
If we suggested, for example, that arrangements be made to bring students here from the French community, which is what the French call their commonwealth, we could run into difficulties with France. I am not sure. But I realize this situation, and we would certainly like to get more French speaking students into Canada.
So that is extremely helpful and I commend the minister for that attitude because I am sure there will be of necessity from the French community students who will want to come here to take post-graduate courses.

Of course there will have to be some kind of arrangement and under this vote there is no such arrangement. The minister has that in mind and that is all to the good; but the point I insist upon and that I come back to is this. Surely if the committee responsible for these scholarships indicates to the commonwealth countries all that the universities of the province of Quebec have to offer there is no doubt in my mind, because of the great culture and the great civilization that is offered by the French Canadian universities in that province, that there are many students, no matter whether they speak languages other than French or English, who will be quite anxious to come and take post-graduate courses at these universities.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should point out that the government does not make the selections in the first place as to what students come, or in the second place as to what universities they attend. That is all handled by the university people themselves.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think I said that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They have a committee on which all of the French speaking universities are represented, which incidentally have been of great help to us. They have their own selection committee made up of representatives from the different universities and we do not interfere with that. We leave it to them to make their own arrangements; but as I said yesterday the difficulty is that most of the different parts of the commonwealth are English speaking. This is what makes for the imbalance.
We are now trying to work out some way to change that situation and, as I said yesterday, in the case of the French community which is composed of various French speaking nations this would have to be arranged through their governments. We do not want to get into difficulties with France and it may take some working out. At the moment I am not clear just how it could be done.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Having regard to the fact that in Canada and in many parts of the world today there is a great engouement- and the minister knows what I mean because now that he is Secretary of State for External Affairs he has improved his French a great deal-for French and French culture, and I am sure he could be of great assistance to us in that respect.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I will draw this to the attention of the university committee and see if they cannot get better results.

Mr. Chairman, I believe there is a point that has been missed in the discussion that the students who attend the University of Montreal or the university of Laval can write their examinations in English and that in many cases the instruction was bilingual. It is not the same, for example, at the University of Manitoba. I know one hon. member of this house who had a son who took a course in architecture. He was not allowed the privilege of writing his examinations in French and as a result he had to quit the course. However, in Quebec students who can write better in English are permitted to write their examinations in English. I think that should do away with the objections that there are few French speaking students coming from commonwealth nations.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I merely want to add a few words to the remarks just made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) in connection with the commonwealth scholarship program, which I entirely approve, as a most interesting development.
According to page 6290 of the official record of July 14, 1960, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) rightly stated:
I sometimes worry about the extent of the interest being taken in external affairs across the country.
And, a little further on, he added:
... yet if a country is to take an active part in world affairs-certainly a country which is under a democratic type of government-it is vital that there be a wide awareness across the country of the different policies involved.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I feel that this amount of $500,000 voted for this scholarship program would certainly contribute to strengthen the ties between the various commonwealth countries. Consequently, I presume that the young students who come from those countries, and also the young Canadians who visit some parts of the commonwealth, will, when they return home, feel it their duty to give lectures so that their fellow citizens will get a better knowledge of the countries where they stayed and of happenings in those areas of the world.
Mr. Chairman, I know that, since the United Nations were established in 1945, the government of the day has been sending delegates and observers there every year, who considered it their duty to give lectures in
Supply-External Affairs social clubs, universities and various towns in their riding. Such policy certainly had the effect of increasing interest in external affairs among our fellow citizens, because, unfortunately, as the minister rightly indicated, our people do not pay enough attention to such important matters as Canada's external affairs.
It gives me pleasure, therefore, to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Laurier, that French language universities be allowed to play a more important part in this scholarship plan.
It is indeed unfortunate to note that our French language universities are getting only 4 or 7 of the 104 representatives who will be coming to study in Canada. I am not blaming the present minister, because in the speech he made this morning, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) referred to the difficulties in finding French language students who might enrol in our universities.
I realize that the plan is now limited to commonwealth countries, but I wonder whether it could not be extended to the various NATO countries, one of which, as the minister knows, is France. Perhaps there would be a case, in the circumstances, for exchanging students with the French Republic; such a program would enable our French speaking students to pursue their studies in that country. If the minister found that there were too many difficulties in the way of setting up such a program, he might refer the matter to the United Nations.
That organization has various agencies, and I wonder if, in fact, it would not be a good idea for the minister to submit this proposal to the United Nations, which might set up another agency if necessary, so that every member country of the United Nations might exchange students of various languages. This step would probably provide a solution to the very difficult problem which has risen, apart from enabling Canada's French language universities to share more actively in this scholarship program.
Mr. Chairman, I am making those suggestions in the best of spirit, and I know the minister will consider it his duty to study them, so that our universities which, as the minister knows, have an excellent reputation, not only in this country but throughout the world, may be in a position to make known the courses they offer or the importance of the role they can play in this country.

93. Contribution to the program of the United Nations high commissioner for refugees, $290,000.

On this vote I want to express my appreciation to the parliamentary secretary to the minister for the very informative address he gave yesterday on item 1 concerning this question of refugees. I believe the hon. member expressed concern that I might have done the campaign for contributions to world refugee year a bit of harm in a number of the remarks I made in that regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said I hoped it would not.

I hope that anything I said hitherto has not harmed a project that has


been reasonably successful and that has provided several million additional dollars to aid refugees. The hon. gentleman did not completely understand my point. We have permitted white refugees to come to Canada from Europe but the refugees in the Middle East are no better off than they ever were. They have been there for a long time. Canadians making contributions to world refugee year out of the goodness of their hearts I believe expected the government to be equitable in expending the money. The money should not be used exclusively to aid white refugees in Europe.
I do not think it is possible for us to continue to maintain the status quo with respect to refugees in the Middle East. An effort has to be made to resolve this problem. If we are prepared to allow 100 tubercular white refugees to enter Canada from Europe I see no reason why we should not allow an equal number to enter Canada from the Middle East or Hong Kong.
On the television screen you see depicted the horrible plight of refugees in Hong Kong. Canada makes no contribution toward their care whatever. We make a contribution to the white refugees from China. I admit that we have admitted many white refugees from Asia and rightly so. We have admitted white refugees out of the European camps and we make a contribution to the maintenance of refugees in the Middle East that only enables them to keep body and soul together. We must do more for the Middle East. The discrimination concerning their entry into Canada should be removed and I hope it will be after the final enactment of the bill of rights. If we are not willing to admit them to Canada we should insist that more should be done for them and we should do more ourselves. The problem of the Middle East will not be resolved as long as there are one million refugees living along the borders of Israel. Canada and other nations will have to spend much more money on this problem than is now being spent.
Canada makes no contribution whatever to non-white refugees in Hong Kong. I do not know why, but apparently this is mainly the responsibility of the government of the United Kingdom. It is not right for us to publicize the plight of refugees in Hong Kong to wring the hearts of kind Canadians in obtaining donations from them if we are unwilling to spend money on behalf of these refugees. Our immigration laws do not permit the entry to Canada from Hong Kong of the non-white relatives of Canadians. We must do more than we are doing to assist in the rehabilitation of these refugees.

I know we cannot admit all the refugees from Hong Kong and I do not propose that. We cannot admit all the refugees from western Europe either. However, if we can admit 100 from western Europe we should be prepared to admit from Hong Kong an equal number of refugees who wish to migrate to Canada but who are now forced to live in the gutters of Hong Kong.

I have a few remarks to make on this vote; I trust it is the appropriate one. I have been asked to bring up the problem of certain former Polish persons who are citizens of Canada, or intend to become citizens of Canada, who were cruelly and badly treated by the nazi authorities during the occupation of Poland. Since that time they have made representations along their own lines and on their own understanding of the law in West Germany for compensation from that government. I have had letters from the Polish congress; I have met representatives of the Polish people in this country and a number of other persons interested in their cause. I am rising, Mr. Chairman, because I do think that we

Supply-Esternal Affairs should do all we can to assist these most unfortunate people who suffered this cruelty and mistreatment because of their opposition to the nazi tyranny and government.
In Britain the victims of nazi barbarism have made representations to the British government, and the matter was raised in the British House of Commons on April 6 of this year when the following exchange occurred:
Sir L. Plummer asked the secretary of state for foreign affairs if he will request the German government to publish the details of the special fund for stateless victims of nazi persecution which is being established by them.
Then, Mr. Allan replied:
The fund has not yet been set up by the German government, so no details are yet available. I have read Dr. Chmielowsky's memorandum and can assure my hon. friend that we are doing our best to promote a fair and early settlement for the stateless refugees.
Then, later, Sir L. Plummer asks again- he is a Conservative, but obviously has humanitarian instincts and is anxious to do what he can for these poor people:
Is the minister aware that those of us who are concerned with the problem are grateful to his right hon. and learned friend for the considerable efforts he has made with the federal government? Nevertheless, may I ask the joint undersecretary to say to his right hon. and learned friend that it is time that pressure was put upon the federal government to make clear to the 25,000 victims of nazi persecution who are stateless and the 1,050 people who suffered from the medical experiments that were made upon them, what compensation they will get for their loss of liberty and loss of health?

I know that my right hon. and learned friend will be grateful for the hon. gentleman's remarks. I can tell him that my right hon. friend the minister of state yesterday sent for the German ambassador and discussed this with him.
I like the word "sent". I might say in this connection I have a number of documents here on my desk; I have consulted with representatives of these victims and I have read a copy of their presentation to the government of West Germany. I have read this material very carefully. When one reads the decisions of the courts in relation to these applications for assistance under German law, his sense of decency and justice is outraged. I do not know whether it is because a few of these blinking nazis are still in quite prominent positions in the courts of Germany; lousy is what they are but we must not kowtow to their injustice. Let me read some extracts from this memorandum:
Poles who were subjected to forced labour in conditions similar to detention encounter the argument that this was no persecution for national reasons, but a measure caused by shortage of labour.
Another Pole encounters the argument that he was dragged into a concentration camp, not as a Pole, but by reason of suspicion of his belonging to a resistance group.

In other words, a member of a resistance group against the German invaders, a patriot.
I continue:
A Polish activist of the radical left, who is seriously ill, is refused any compensation on the grounds that he "certainly" endangered the occupying power. No proof of this was supplied.
A 13 year old child was brought into a concentration camp because the mother had been arrested, allegedly for security reasons. Result: no compensation for the child.
I feel very strongly about this sort of thing, Mr. Chairman, because I have met some of these people. I am informed that the government of Great Britain is officially taking up cases of people who come under their jurisdiction in Great Britain, with the West German government. I urge that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and our officials do what they can to assist these persons, some of whom are citizens of Canada.
I have sent a list of the names to the secretary of state to see that we do whatever we can in order that they obtain justice. I am told that in many cases the answer on the part of the West German government is that these people are not now citizens of Germany and the answer of other governments -I do not know whether our government has made this answer-is that the damages occurred in a country other than that in which these people are now living. These poor people who suffered as a result of nazi persecution and cruelty are as it were shuffled between two points of view and in many cases on that account have been unable to obtain justice. I urge the government to do all it can to persuade the West German government to treat these people fairly according to the text of the law in West Germany with respect to compensation.

I should like to say a word in support of the position taken by the hon. member. I have also had some contact with some of these people and I know how they feel about this matter. I know that as Canadian citizens who have suffered from nazi persecution they are entitled to intervention on their behalf by our government, and I would hope that the minister and the department will do everything they can by that kind of intervention with the West German government to see that they get justice. Anything the government can do in that regard will certainly be warmly supported on this side of the house.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We have the details now of the cases of a number of these unfortunate people and we are checking the situation and will do what we can to help them.

Mr. Chairman, I want to bring one matter to the attention of the minister. I have already raised it in the house and that is why I can be brief today. It has to do with a decision of the international joint commission and with a matter which I brought to the attention of the Minister of Transport. He very kindly said that inasmuch as he could make representations to the international joint commission and to his colleague he would do so. I believe that the minister has already done so and if he has not I am sure he will. Here is what the matter concerns.
When the international joint commission decided to approve the joint power and seaway development in the international section at Cornwall they made an order of approval, and the order of approval is quite clear. I wish to put two short paragraphs of the order of approval on the record so that the minister will get the gist of my remarks. The order of approval was subject to several conditions, and I should like to refer to two of them. It was ordered that the project be approved of subject to these conditions, among others:
(a)	All interests on either side of the international boundary which are injured by reason of the construction, maintenance and operation of the works shall be given suitable and adequate protection and indemnity in accordance with the laws in Canada or the constitution and laws in the United States.
I would ask the minister to listen to this, if he would be so kind, because I think it means a great deal to the area concerned.
(b)	The works shall be so planned, located, constructed, maintained and operated as not to conflict with or restrain uses of the waters of the St. Lawrence river for purposes given preference over uses of water for power purposes by the treaty, namely, uses for domestic and sanitary purposes and uses for navigation, including the service of canals for the purposes of navigation, and shall be so planned, located, constructed, maintained and operated as to give effect to the provisions of this order.
What does all this mean? It means that the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario, because of power development, are not allowing the required amount of water to go down the Cornwall canal with the result that there is serious stagnation of the water and an unhygienic condition which has been condemned by the medical officer of health in that area, which was responsible for an epidemic of eye soreness last year and which has caused the closing down of all the bathing spots within that area. In one word, prior to the opening of navigation the velocity of 79951-0-403
Supply-External Affairs the canal was eight cubic feet per second. Because of the power development it has been reduced to four cubic feet per second.
There is a sewer that empties into the canal and always has for years and the velocity of eight feet per second carried away that waste without the slightest trouble or the slightest injury or damage to health. But now, because of the reduction from eight to four feet per second, the position is untenable from the point of view of the velocity, from the point of view of hygiene and from the point of view of this sewer outlet from a whole subdivision adjacent to the city of Cornwall, with the result that this order of the international joint commission is being directly infringed.
When the matter was brought to the attention of the Minister of Transport he seemed to think it was a matter that should be brought to the attention of his colleague. I am interested in the question particularly because I was present at the public hearings in the city of Cornwall prior to the making of the order of approval and the position was clearly stated by the international joint commission. I am sure the commission agrees fully with the position I am taking now because this situation comes within the terms of their order.
There is a way of dealing with the matter which would make things much easier for all parties concerned rather than giving directions, making orders and so forth. If the international joint commission will bring this matter to the attention of Ontario hydro and tell them they are contravening this order I think this will be the end of it. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know the committee will be very glad to get away from the contentious realm of external affairs and enter the quiet, pacific water of public works. I shall be very brief in my introductory remarks. However, of necessity, because there are so many figures, I shall have to pay close attention to my notes, far closer than I usually do, but probably with better effect.
Most of the questions concerning the estimates of the Department of Public Works which hon. members will want to discuss can best be dealt with, I know, on the individual items and that is the way you prefer it rather than an introductory statement. I think, however, with your permission I should like to indicate to you some of the salient points of interest. My remarks will be made under three headings: First, a summary of the noteworthy features in the departmental operation in the 1959-60 fiscal year; second, the highlights of the public works program for 1960-61; and, third, an explanation of the reductions in the estimates for 1960-61 compared with those of 1959-60.
Dealing with No. 1, a review of the operations of 1959-60, I may say the total appropriations for 1959-60, both statutory and non-statutory, amounted to $233.5 million. The expenditures in 1959-60 were $211.7 million, which is approximately 90.7 per cent of the amount requested. Judging by the department's activities in past years, this is a good record. The ratio between expenditures. that is work carried out and total estimates, work planned, has been as low as 70 per cent in 1952-53 and as high as 97 per cent under my predecessor the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, during 1957-58.
Expenditures on public buildings in 195960 were $44.1 million, and on harbour and river projects, $28 million. Payments to provincial governments for the federal government's share of trans-Canada highway construction were $53.2 million, an increase of $2 million over the previous fiscal year. This is the largest expenditure that has been made on the trans-Canada highway in any fiscal year so far. The amounts for previous years were $51.1 million, 1958-59; $49.4 million, 1957-58; and $24.8 million, 1956-57. Then, of course, there are expenditures on the trans-Canada highway through national parks 79951-0-4034
Supply-Public Works which, as members know, are entirely a federal responsibility and these amounted to $12 million for the year.
During the year 1959-60 contracts were awarded for 55 standard post office buildings across the country under a program explained in some detail by my predecessor during the discussion of public works estimates last year. This program which is now becoming one of a continuing nature has been extremely well received and has resulted not only in improved services but in the addition of handsome small buildings in many of the smaller Canadian communities.
Turning to the larger projects, important buildings were completed during 1959-60 in various centres across the country, and I would just like to review the most important of them.
Newfoundland: The Sir Humphrey Gilbert building and the post office building in St. John's.
Prince Edward Island: The Souris east public building.
New Brunswick: The Grand Falls public building.
Quebec: The national revenue building at Montreal as well as the public building at Sept lies.
Ontario: Public buildings in Belleville and Stratford, a new unemployment insurance commission building at Peterborough and also the Mackenzie building at Toronto.
Manitoba: The customs and immigration facilities at Emerson and a public building at Portage la Prairie.
Saskatchewan: A contract for a new public building at Saskatoon was awarded in November of 1959.
British Columbia: A public building at Port Alberni.
Northwest Territories: A public building at Inuvik.
A number of large projects were completed by the harbours and rivers engineering branch during the year. They include the improvements to the harbour at Port aux Basques, Newfoundland; enlargement of the wharf at Pointe au Pic, Quebec; and dredging at several Ontario ports:	Bay of Quinte
Cobourg, Oshawa and Port Hope. Important dredging and harbour improvement work associated with the seaway at Toronto and Hamilton were also completed or were nearing completion during the year.
Large harbour development programs at the lakehead in Ontario and St. John's, Newfoundland, which take a number of years to complete, made good progress. A good rate of activity was also maintained on harbour

Supply-Public Works improvement works at Pointe au Pere, in Quebec, and at Campbell River and Port Alberni in British Columbia.
Construction of two large bridges, the interprovincial bridge from Campbellton, New Brunswick to Cross Point, Quebec, and the low level canal bridge at Burlington, Ontario, was continued at a good pace during 1959-60.
There was a good increase last year in the construction work done by the Department of Public Works for other government departments with funds provided in their appropriations. From the department's standpoint, this is a source of satisfaction because it indicates increasing confidence by other departments in the ability of public works to meet their requirements, which in some cases are quite specialized. More than 300 projects for a total of 16 departments were handled during the year, and the resulting expenditure was $43.5 million. This is about $10 million higher than the value of work done for other departments in 1958-59.
Public works maintenance and operation activities, which involve not only public buildings but bridges, wharves, graving docks, a testing laboratory and maintenance dredging for navigation, were carried out at a level comparable to that for the previous fiscal year.
Now may I deal with the highlights of the present fiscal year 1960-61. First, with the major projects proceeding at the present time, quite a few major projects which take more than one year to complete will be continued in 1960-61. These include the $13 million St. John's harbour development in Newfoundland, the construction of the large harbour terminal at the head of the lakes and several large buildings. In addition, construction will be started on a number of projects for which planning and preliminary work was done with funds from the 1959-60 estimates. The following are some of the more important projects in this category.
New Brunswick: Moncton, addition and alternations to the public building at an estimated cost of $1,800,000.
Quebec: At Quebec city, a postal terminal. This $3 million project has been delayed because of complicated site negotiations but I am very happy to say they have now been resolved. Tenders have been received and it is expected that construction will commence in a matter of weeks. Then in Montreal there is the new building for the Department of Veterans Affairs at an estimated cost of $1,250,000. Outside the large metropolitan area public buildings are proposed for the communities of Hudson, $30,000; Laval des Rapides, $150,000; and Les Escoumains, $30,000.

Ontario: Similarly, new public buildings are planned for several smaller municipalities in Ontario. At Caledonia, $45,000; Chesterville, $30,000; West Lome, $30,000; Ingersoll, $75,000; and Downsview, $250,000. As to Ottawa, the building program in the capital will include renovations to the west block, which as all hon. members know were begun earlier to provide more accommodation for members of parliament and House of Commons services. As hon. members also know, they wished the exterior appearance of the building to be preserved, although there may be some very minor changes. At Toronto a study of the requirements and preliminary planning will be continued during 1960-61 for a large postal terminal, but no construction will be started. This is very much needed but it takes some time to plan.
Manitoba: At Winnipeg, a new building for the unemployment insurance commission at an estimated cost of $1.5 million.
Alberta: At Edmonton, a major addition and alterations to the postal terminal building at an estimated cost of $4 million, including acquisition of the required site.
British Columbia: At Penticton a new building, $790,000; at Prince Rupert a new public building, $350,000
Yukon and Northwest Territories: Construction of residential housing for federal government employees will be continued during the year at several northern locations. The centres affected are Fort Smith, Inuvik, Yellowknife and Whitehorse.
May I now say a word about the standard post office construction program which has drawn a great deal of commendation from members on both sides of the house. The construction program for these standard post offices in the smaller Canadian communities will be continued. Our tentative plans call for construction at 61 locations during 196061. However, because of factors still not determined, such as acquisition of the sites in some cases, it is not possible to be definite at this time on the total number involved. With the carrying out of this proposed program a total of approximately 175 Canadian communities will have received one of these attractive and useful public buildings since the program began in 1958-59.
Now as to the trans-Canada highway through national parks. In the national parks the responsibility is entirely on the federal government for the construction of the trans-Canada highway and progress in these sections has been quite satisfactory. There is something we can control ourselves, and we are in sole charge of it as well as paying for it. At the present time there is a bituminous pavement throughout Banff and Yoho

national parks and we expect that a bituminous surface will be placed in the Terra Nova park in Newfoundland and also in the Revelstoke sections by the end of the present construction season. This will leave only the section through Glacier national park, and all of it is now under grading contract. We plan to do the paving through Glacier during the 1961 construction season.
Part of the route in Glacier national park, incidentally, passes through avalanche country, and we have had to be particularly careful in our handling of this problem. Several questions have been asked about this from time to time. Research to determine the most effective type of avalanche defence has been going on since 1953, and the results are now being put into effect. This will give us a system of avalanche defences comparable in standards of safety to the best mountain highways in the world.
I might add that an avalanche forecasting system has been in operation in this section for two years now, just as if the road were actually open to traffic, and it has proved to be very accurate indeed. By using this forecasting system and the information obtained by research, the expected time that the highway will be forced to close to traffic during an average year has been reduced to about 12 days. This is much better than we had previously anticipated.
The mile of road which includes these snow sheds, some 2,475 feet of them in all, is undoubtedly the most expensive mile in the whole trans-Canada highway. It is estimated to cost $3.5 million, everything included. For tourist purposes, the new route passes through some of the world's most spectacular mountain scenery, and I have no doubt that hon. members who have been to this part of the country will bear me out in this connection. In addition, the new route will cut more than 100 miles from the length of the trip between Golden and Revelstoke which represents another major advance.
Speaking of the trans-Canada highway, we had a long debate on that when the act was amended, so I shall refer to it only very briefly. Progress on the trans-Canada highway as a whole does, of course, depend on the construction programs of the various provincial highway departments. At present, there are two main gaps in the highway. The first is north of lake Superior, between Agawa and White River, and the other between Revelstoke and Donald in British Columbia. Good progress is expected on both of these sections in the present construction season. The Ontario section is expected to be open to traffic this year, and the British Columbia section may be open in 1961, depending on construction progress. When this happens, our
